high_priority_articles.title: India–New Zealand FTA: Government Notifies First Tranche of Customs Duty Concessions; Preferential Tariffs, TRQs and Import Conditions Effective October 20, 2026 - A2Z Taxcorp LLP
high_priority_articles.summary: India–New Zealand FTA: Government Notifies First Tranche of Customs Duty Concessions; Preferential Tariffs, TRQs and Import Conditions Effective October 20, 2026  A2Z Taxcorp LLP
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), Government of India, has issued Notification No. 32/2026-Customs dated October 16, 2026, notifying the first tranche of tariff concessions under the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (Ind-NZ FTA). The notification, issued under Section 25(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, shall come into force on October 20, 2026.
The notification establishes preferential customs duty treatment for specified goods imported into India from New Zealand, covering concessions in Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC) and Health Cess, as applicable. These concessions are subject to the relevant tariff classifications, product descriptions, value thresholds, quantitative restrictions and prescribed conditions.
Comprehensive Product-Wise Tariff Concessions
Under Table I of the notification, the Government has prescribed preferential customs duty rates for a wide range of tariff lines covering specified agricultural, marine, industrial and other goods. The applicable BCD, AIDC and Health Cess rates have been specified separately for individual tariff classifications.
For instance, imports of fresh, chilled or frozen sheep meat falling under heading 0204 have been assigned a preferential BCD of Nil, AIDC of Nil and Health Cess of Nil. Several specified fish and marine product classifications are also covered by preferential rates, including certain tariff lines carrying a BCD of 25.71%, with Nil AIDC and Health Cess.
The applicable concessions vary across products and tariff lines. Accordingly, importers must examine the precise tariff classification and corresponding rate prescribed under the notification before claiming preferential treatment.
Preferential Customs Duty on Wines Based on CIF Value
Under Table II, the Government has introduced value-based preferential tariff treatment for specified wine products imported from New Zealand.
For the specified tariff classifications covering wines, including sparkling wines and other listed wine products, the notification prescribes the following concessions based on the CIF value of a 750 ml container:
- CIF value of US$5 or above but below US$15: BCD of 20% and AIDC of 75%.
- CIF value of US$15 or above: BCD of 20% and AIDC of 50%.
The preferential rates are subject to the relevant tariff classifications and product descriptions. The notification clarifies that the CIF value shall mean the assessable value determined under Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962.
Special Preferential Duty Treatment for Kiwifruit and Mānuka Honey
Under Table III, specific preferential duty rates have been notified for New Zealand-origin kiwifruit and Mānuka honey satisfying the prescribed import value conditions.
For kiwifruit falling under HS Code 08105000, having a CIF value of US$2.50 per kg or above, the applicable preferential BCD shall be 15%, with Nil AIDC.
Similarly, Mānuka honey falling under HS Code 04090000, having a CIF value of US$30 per kg or above, shall attract a preferential BCD of 51%, with Nil AIDC, subject to the prescribed certification condition.
For Mānuka honey, the importer must produce a certificate issued by the Ministry for Primary Industries, New Zealand, certifying the imported product as Mānuka honey.
Tariff Rate Quotas Introduced for Mānuka Honey and Albumins
Under Table IV, the notification prescribes Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) concessions for specified imports, enabling eligible quantities of goods to be imported at the notified in-quota customs duty rates, subject to DGFT authorisation and customs compliance requirements.
For Mānuka honey under HS Code 04090000, having a CIF value of US$20 per kg or above but below US$30 per kg, an initial TRQ quantity of 40 metric tonnes has been notified, with an in-quota BCD of 51% and Nil AIDC.
For albumins falling under HS Codes 35021100, 35021900, 35022000 and 35029000, a TRQ quantity of 200 metric tonnes has been prescribed, attracting an in-quota BCD of 10% and Nil AIDC.
These quantities form part of the initial tariff concession framework under the FTA, with the related quota allocation and implementation procedures governed by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).
Mandatory DGFT Authorisation and Electronic Customs Monitoring
The notification stipulates that importers seeking concessional benefits under the applicable TRQ provisions must obtain authorisation from DGFT in accordance with the relevant procedures prescribed under the Handbook of Procedures, 2023.
The TRQ authorisation must contain the name and address of the importer, Importer-Exporter Code (IEC), relevant Customs Notification number, applicable tariff item, authorised quantity and validity period.
Such authorisations shall be issued electronically by DGFT and transmitted to the Indian Customs EDI System (ICES). Imports against TRQ authorisations shall be permitted only after the corresponding quantities have been debited electronically through ICES.
The electronic authorisation and debit mechanism is intended to facilitate administration and monitoring of the notified tariff quotas.
Rules of Origin Compliance Mandatory to Avail FTA Benefits
A significant condition under the notification is that the preferential customs duty concessions shall be available only for qualifying goods originating in New Zealand.
Importers must establish the origin of imported goods to the satisfaction of the jurisdictional Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner of Customs, in accordance with the Customs (Administration of Rules of Origin under Trade Agreements) Rules, 2020 (CAROTAR, 2020) and other applicable rules notified by the Central Government.
Accordingly, the mere import of goods from New Zealand shall not automatically entitle an importer to preferential customs duty treatment unless the prescribed origin requirements and relevant conditions are satisfied.
Implementation from October 20, 2026
The concessional customs duty rates and prescribed TRQ provisions under Notification No. 32/2026-Customs dated October 16, 2026 shall become applicable from October 20, 2026.
The notification operates alongside DGFT Public Notice No. 33/2026-27 dated October 17, 2026, which amends Paragraph 2.92 and Appendix 2A of the Handbook of Procedures, 2023, to prescribe the procedural framework for TRQ allocations under the India–New Zealand FTA.
Together, the customs notification and DGFT procedural amendments establish the framework for extending preferential import treatment and administering tariff quotas under the Agreement.
Significance for Indian Importers and Trade
The implementation of the first tranche of tariff concessions under the India–New Zealand FTA represents an important development in bilateral trade policy and preferential customs administration.
The concessions may create additional opportunities for eligible New Zealand-origin goods to enter the Indian market at preferential tariff rates, while the prescribed value thresholds, tariff classifications, quantitative restrictions and origin requirements provide safeguards for administering the concessions.
For Indian importers, customs brokers and businesses engaged in international trade, the notification makes it essential to carefully evaluate HS classification, applicable preferential BCD and cess rates, CIF value thresholds, origin documentation, DGFT authorisation and electronic quota compliance, wherever applicable.
The notification marks an important step in operationalising the first tranche of tariff commitments under the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, with preferential customs duty benefits becoming effective from October 20, 2026.

FOMC Polymarket odds increasingly favor the Federal Reserve leaving interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, with the probability of another rate hike falling sharply despite persistent inflation concerns.
According to the latest Polymarket figures, the odds of the Fed holding rates steady stand at 87%, while the probability of a 25-basis-point increase has dropped to 14%. The market assigns less than a 1% chance to a rate cut or a larger increase.
The figures suggest traders expect Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to take a wait-and-see approach at their October 27–28 meeting. The contract has attracted tens of millions of dollars in trading volume, reflecting significant interest in the central bank’s next move.
However, expectations have shifted considerably in recent weeks. After hotter-than-expected inflation data, the probability of an October hike climbed toward 50% before retreating as investors reassessed the likelihood of consecutive hikes.
FOMC Polymarket Odds: Inflation Keeps Rate Hike Debate Alive
The latest US consumer price index (CPI) report showed annual inflation accelerating to 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Core inflation also increased, reinforcing concerns that price pressures could remain above the Fed’s 2% target.
Nevertheless, some policymakers have argued against rushing into another increase. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on October 14 that further hikes could be necessary to control persistent inflation but stressed there was no urgency to act at the upcoming meeting.
That distinction appears central to current market pricing: traders are not ruling out additional tightening, but increasingly expect policymakers to wait for more evidence before moving again.

- Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.
- Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones.
- Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”
- In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage. In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.
- Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed, a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced the controversial agreement with Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”
- Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- Russia’s defence ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a “massive strike” on targets in Kyiv and the Ukraine’s capital region. The ministry said the attack targeted military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones and data centres. Earlier, Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said a Russian air strike had killed one person and injured two in the city overnight. A medical facility and a non-residential building were damaged in the attack, he said.
- A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday, officials said. Ukraine’s foreign ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.

high_priority_articles.title: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried. - Latin Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried.  Latin Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Vietnam did not wait for Latin America to catch up.
While South American and Mexican exporters were still absorbing the ripple effects of their own hard-won market openings, Hanoi moved — completing a sweeping trade pact with Europe's second commercial bloc one day after the rest of the world's attention was focused elsewhere. The consequences for Latin American manufacturers are not theoretical; they are structural, and they are already in motion.
A 14-Year Deal With Immediate Market Consequences
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association formally concluded a comprehensive free trade agreement on October 18, 2026, in Hanoi, after fourteen years and 21 rounds of negotiations that began in 2012 and were interrupted for years before resuming in 2025. The ceremony brought together Lê Mạnh Hùng, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, who signed the document on Hanoi's behalf, alongside the heads of government of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein.
President and General Secretary Tô Lâm — Vietnam's top leader, holding the country's two most powerful positions simultaneously — attended the Hanoi ceremony in person, a signal that this was not a routine trade formality but a presidential-level strategic commitment.
The scope of the agreement is broad: it addresses trade in goods and services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights, government procurement, investment, sanitary measures, and sustainable development. But it is the tariff architecture that carries the most immediate competitive weight.
Under the deal, EFTA members immediately liberalize more than 90% of tariff lines, representing 99.5% of Vietnam's current exports to the bloc. Covered products include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers and electronic components, and machinery and equipment. Vietnamese agricultural goods — including rice, honey, and fruit — also receive tariff reductions. Selected European products such as cheese and chocolate will gain duty-free access to the Vietnamese market, but only after a transition period of up to 16 years.
The EFTA Prize: A $630 Billion Market With Room to Grow
The commercial opportunity at stake is considerable. EFTA's annual import turnover runs to roughly $630 billion, and Vietnamese goods currently account for just 0.65% of that figure. Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam totaled €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam running a €2.5 billion surplus — a gap that has widened sharply compared with a decade earlier.
For Colombian garment producers, Brazilian footwear exporters, and Mexican electronics assemblers competing for shelf space in Zurich or Oslo, the arithmetic is straightforward: their Vietnamese rivals now pay zero import duties, while Latin American goods still face standard EFTA tariff rates. The competitive floor has shifted, and there is no reversal mechanism built into the agreement.
The Mercosur Flank: Vietnam Takes the Competition South
The EFTA pact drew the headlines, but a simultaneous diplomatic push may ultimately prove more consequential for the region. Vietnam is negotiating directly with South America's largest economic bloc — not just for market access in Europe, but for preferential access to Mercosur's domestic markets themselves.
The first round of negotiations for the Vietnam–Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement concluded on August 28, 2026, after five days of technical sessions in Buenos Aires, with Argentina coordinating the bloc's side. The framing on both ends was optimistic: Argentine officials highlighted that bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, growing from approximately $6.6 billion in 2015 to more than $12 billion in 2025, without any preferential framework in place.
If a preferential deal is reached, the implications for Brazilian and Argentine manufacturers extend beyond export competition in third markets. Vietnamese electronics — which generated nearly $165 billion in export revenue in 2025 — would gain improved access to the Brazilian and Argentine consumer market, the very domestic revenue base that regional producers depend on when global export conditions tighten.
Latin American Textiles and Electronics Face a Structural Squeeze
For the textile sector on both continents, the combined effect of Vietnam's European trade moves represents a pincer movement.
Brazil's textile and apparel industry counts 25,700 businesses employing approximately 1.3 million workers and generating $40.9 billion in annual revenue. The sector had cautiously welcomed the EU–Mercosur agreement — signed in Asunción on January 17, 2026 — as a pathway to expanded European market access. Industry associations representing Brazilian manufacturers (ABIT), their Argentine counterparts (FITA), and Europe's own textile lobby (EURATEX) issued a joint statement in February calling the deal "essential" for competitiveness on both sides of the Atlantic.
Vietnam's EFTA deal partially neutralizes that advantage. European buyers who might have shifted sourcing toward Mercosur suppliers under the new EU framework now have an equally competitive Vietnamese alternative — one that operates under zero tariffs across both EU and EFTA channels simultaneously.
The overlap in export categories is not coincidental. Vietnam's textile and garment industry posted $46 billion in exports in 2025 and has set a $50 billion target for 2026, driven by the same European and American buyers that Latin American producers compete for. Vietnam is already the world's second-largest garment exporter. The EFTA deal adds one more preferential lane to a network that already covers most of its major trading partners.
Hanoi's Export Pivot and the U.S. Tariff Pressure
The aggressive pace of trade diversification is not a coincidence of timing. Vietnam has been under sustained pressure to reduce its dependence on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 30% of Vietnam's total exports. That reliance became a structural liability after Washington imposed reciprocal tariffs that left Vietnamese textile and garment exports facing a 12.5% U.S. import duty — 2.5 percentage points above the 10% rate applied to some regional competitors — according to the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association.
Vietnam's response has been systematic: conclude the EFTA deal, push for EU-market access under the existing EU–Vietnam FTA (in force since 2020), and now open negotiations with Mercosur. Taken together, the strategy is to spread export volume across so many preferential lanes that no single market disruption — however large — can destabilize the country's export-driven growth model.
What Latin American Trade Ministries Must Reckon With Now
The Vietnam–Mercosur PTA remains at an early stage, and the EFTA deal must pass parliamentary ratification in each member country before entering full force. But direction matters as much as timeline in trade policy, and the direction here is unambiguous.
Vietnam is no longer simply an Asian competitor in Asian-facing supply chains. It is now an active rival in European markets — and a prospective entrant to South American domestic ones. For trade ministries from Bogotá to São Paulo, the question is no longer whether to respond; it is how fast a coordinated response can be assembled, and whether the advantages secured under the EU–Mercosur agreement will be enough to offset what Hanoi has just put in place.

high_priority_articles.title: Intel's $200 Million Bet on EUV Paid Off for ASML and TSMC, Not Intel - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: Intel's $200 Million Bet on EUV Paid Off for ASML and TSMC, Not Intel  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
When Intel's top executives gathered in CEO Andy Grove's office in 1992, the agenda was not a celebration but a crisis. The company had reclaimed the title of world's largest semiconductor maker on the strength of its central processing units (CPUs), but Moore's Law — the principle that circuit density doubles every two years — was running into technical limits. The conclusion from the meeting was blunt: "There is no way forward."
The person who offered a breakthrough was John Carruthers, who headed Intel's manufacturing process research. Having moved to Intel after developing component materials at NASA, he proposed building a new kind of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machine. It was the starting point for the equipment that today is indispensable to producing AI semiconductors and high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
Lithography equipment works like a photo enlarger, shining light through a mask to etch circuit patterns onto a wafer. The deep ultraviolet (DUV) tools Intel used at the time passed light with a wavelength of 198 nanometers through lenses to draw circuits. What Carruthers focused on was extreme ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers. The shorter the wavelength, the finer the circuit that can be drawn — much like a sharper pencil tip. Industry experts say DUV struggles to reliably print circuits below 7 nanometers, and that exposing the wafer multiple times erodes yields.
The problem was that such a machine did not exist. The amount Carruthers asked Grove for was $200 million (about 270 billion won). Grove balked at investing in something with no guarantee of success, but Carruthers was adamant: without it, there would be no way to develop semiconductors any further.
In 1997, Intel formed a public-private consortium with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under the U.S. Department of Energy, Motorola and AMD to jointly develop core EUV technology. But commercializing the technology required a company to build the machines. The U.S. equipment industry, having lost ground to Japanese semiconductor companies in the 1980s, had all but collapsed, and even the largest remaining player, Silicon Valley Group, lacked the technology to build EUV tools.
At the time, the dominant players in the lithography market were Japan's Canon and Nikon. But the U.S. government, wary of technology leaks after its bruising experience with Japanese companies, would not allow cooperation with Japanese manufacturers. The alternative Intel found was ASML, a small Dutch company. ASML, which counted Micron as a major customer and was developing its own EUV equipment, joined the Intel-led consortium in the early 2000s.
ASML was originally spun off in 1984 from Philips' semiconductor division. Whereas Japan's semiconductor industry took a closed approach, trying to source equipment and components domestically, ASML grew by absorbing technology and parts from companies around the world. The fact that Taiwan's TSMC was a customer from the company's early days also proved decisive later: Philips invested in TSMC and provided manufacturing technology, which naturally led to ASML equipment being used there.
The Intel-ASML combination pushed Japanese companies out of the race for core EUV technology. Canon and Nikon abandoned equipment development, leaving ASML as the world's sole supplier of EUV lithography machines. ASML cemented its monopoly by acquiring even Silicon Valley Group in 2001. The "another tiger cub" that the U.S. government had feared had become a reality.
In the end, it was South Korea's Samsung Electronics and Taiwan's TSMC, not Intel, that first walked through the EUV door that Intel had opened with its money and organization. EUV is now a core tool in Samsung's advanced foundry processes and in SK Hynix's HBM production lines. Intel, the driving force behind the core technology, was left as a latecomer in the mass-production race, forced to compete for EUV equipment allocations.
This shift in technological leadership is playing out again in today's investment landscape for the semiconductor industry. As the race to shrink process nodes nears its limits, the battleground is moving back to back-end processing. TSMC plans to keep its capital expenditure forecast for this year at $60 billion to $64 billion (about 79.8 trillion to 85.1 trillion won), allocating 10% to 20% of that to advanced packaging, testing and photomask production. The key focus is expanding CoWoS capacity, which packages GPUs and HBM together.
Investment by back-end specialists is also growing. Taiwan's ASE Technology Holding raised its capital expenditure plan for this year from $8.5 billion (about 11.3 trillion won) to $10.5 billion (about 14 trillion won), while U.S.-based Amkor announced a second-phase expansion of its Arizona campus, lifting total investment to about $12 billion (about 16 trillion won). In memory, South Korea's SK Hynix is building HBM advanced packaging production facilities in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, and in West Lafayette, Indiana, targeting mass production by late 2029. Micron is investing about $7 billion (about 9.3 trillion won) in Singapore to build an HBM packaging hub.
Market research firm Yole Group projects that the global advanced packaging market will more than double from $55 billion (about 73.2 trillion won) in 2025 to more than $120 billion (about 159.6 trillion won) by 2031. It also forecast that advanced packaging will account for more than half of total semiconductor packaging revenue by 2031.
The lesson from the EUV saga is that the value of a technology shifts to whoever applies it to mass production first. The fact that the market went not to the company that funded the core technology but to the one that turned it into equipment and built a mass-production system with customers could well repeat in today's advanced packaging race. Where the value chain forms across equipment, materials and inspection and testing is seen as the variable that will determine the direction of the next-generation AI semiconductor supply chain.

(Kitco News) – Gold and silver both came under renewed pressure following last week’s elevated CPI and PPI prints. Still, gold ETF demand has bucked the earlier trend to rise to annual highs despite the oil and rate headwinds. At the same time, India’s evolving import tax rules continue to impact precious metals demand, according to precious metals analysts at Heraeus.
In their latest update, the analysts noted that gold prices held critical support levels last week amidst a challenging macro backdrop.
“Gold briefly wicked below $4,100/oz following the September US CPI release, as the initially hawkish market reaction pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher and increased expectations for another Fed hike,” they noted. “That reaction has since partly reversed, with the implied probability of a 25 bp increase at the 28 October meeting falling and gold recovering the support at $4,100/oz as yields and the dollar have eased.”
Gold ETF holdings have also climbed to their highest levels of the year to date despite the significant pressures on the gold price.
“Bloomberg-tracked holdings reached a year-to-date peak of 101.3 moz on 8 October, up 5.3% from the year-to-date low of 96.2 moz on 20 July and around 2% higher than at the start of the year,” the analysts noted. “Holdings have since remained just above 101 moz, even as gold has struggled at around $4,100-4,200/oz, well below its January peak.”
“For much of 2026, changes in ETF holdings have broadly tracked the gold price, falling during the correction from the January high before recovering as prices rebounded through August, but the two have since diverged,” they said. “ETF holdings often lag turning points in the price, as investors tend to hold positions, or add on dips, in anticipation of a renewed rally until it becomes clear that one is not imminent. Demand has also broadened geographically, with Asian-listed funds accounting for almost half of the increase in global holdings over the 12 months to September, compared with around 30% from US-listed funds and 20% from Europe.”
And after being among the largest sovereign buyers of 2026, the central bank of Kazakhstan is reducing its gold holdings.
“The National Bank of Kazakhstan plans to lower gold's share of its international reserves from around 78% to 75% by year-end, after holdings climbed to 386 tonnes,” the analysts said. “The bank was the world's fourth-largest reported central-bank buyer through August, adding around 36 tonnes during the first eight months of the year. The planned reduction will be split between options and sales of physical bullion, as elevated US Treasury yields increase the relative appeal of dollar assets and the central bank seeks to reduce concentration risk in its reserves.”
“At current reserve values, a 3-percentage-point reduction in gold's share would represent roughly 15 tonnes of gold exposure, although the amount of physical metal sold will depend on prices and the use of derivatives,” they noted. “The move is therefore primarily a portfolio rebalancing exercise rather than evidence of a broader reversal in central-bank gold demand.”
Spot gold continued to trade near session lows early in the early part of the North American session, and last traded at $4,151.80 per ounce for a loss of 0.33% on the daily chart.
Turning to silver, Heraeus analysts pointed out that the gray metal was also under pressure following last week’s hotter-than-expected inflation reports.
“The silver price fell through support around $60/oz and briefly approached the July lows around $55/oz, as the data strengthened expectations for another Fed rate hike and initially pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher,” they said. “That reaction has subsequently eased, with the implied probability of a 25 bp increase at the 28 October meeting falling to below 30%, while the 10-year Treasury yield and dollar have both moved lower, down from recent yearly highs. Silver consequently recovered above $57/oz, although the break below $60/oz leaves the technical picture weaker and highlights the metal’s sensitivity to changes in real yields and monetary-policy expectations.”
And India’s import tax regime for precious metals continues to evolve, impacting banks and wholesale demand.
“The Indian government has confirmed that silver, gold and platinum imports by banks and nominated agencies are subject to 3% Integrated Goods and Services Tax,” the analysts wrote. “The government said on 8 October that the exemption for these channels had not been extended beyond 31 March, putting all import routes on an equal tax footing. Banks have, in practice, been paying the tax since April, after a month-long pause in imports while the rules were unclear. As the levy is recoverable as an input tax credit, its main effect is on working capital rather than final costs, and the confirmation removes uncertainty rather than adding a new obstacle to Indian silver imports. India imported 232 moz of silver in 2025, equivalent to around 20% of global demand.”

high_priority_articles.title: China’s non-tariff walls a major export hurdle: FM Nirmala Sitharaman - India Shipping News
high_priority_articles.summary: China’s non-tariff walls a major export hurdle: FM Nirmala Sitharaman  India Shipping News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
BANGKOK: Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday said China’s non-tariff barriers were the biggest hurdle for Indian exports, alleging that Beijing had denied market access to Indian products despite significant demand potential, including for generic drugs, bovine meat and agricultural produce, contributing to a widening trade imbalance. She also called for a review of India’s trade agreement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), saying its benefits were skewed in favour of the bloc.
“A decade has gone by consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products but non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly. Non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” she said during a conversation hosted by the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
India’s trade deficit with China more than doubled to $112 billion in FY26 from $52.7 billion in FY16. Sitharaman said New Delhi had repeatedly sought market access for products in which India had a competitive advantage, but progress had been limited despite scope for discussions on sanitary and phytosanitary measures and other regulatory issues.
Responding to Sitharaman’s remarks, China’s foreign ministry said Beijing was ready to work with New Delhi to address “each other’s economic and trade concerns in a balanced way and promote the steady development of bilateral relations”. “China never aims for trade surplus,” Chinese foreign ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning told media in Beijing, as reported by PTI.
Sitharaman’s comments come days after Commerce Minister Shri Piyush Goyal said India was working to develop relations with China “once again”, while cautioning that the outcome remained uncertain.
“I think we had some concerns in the past. We are working to develop relations with China once again, but the last word has not been scripted on this journey,” he said on Wednesday at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum.
Sitharaman said India had refrained from adopting punitive trade measures to address its trade imbalance with China, preferring negotiations despite the difficulties involved, unlike some other countries. “Probably that’s not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome but we do go through that approach rather than putting countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter their non-tariff barriers,” she said.
On the skew in trade benefits in favour of Asean, Sitharaman said India needed to reassess the impact of its trade agreement with the bloc, signed more than a decade ago, and refashion it to address the imbalance and its effects on domestic manufacturers and importers. “We need to have that agreement continue but in a slightly refashioned manner. It cannot so adversely affect one side which is the Indian side,” she said. India’s trade deficit with Asean countries crossed $50 billion in FY26.
Sitharaman also defended India’s decision to stay out of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), saying the government had not seen sufficient benefits in joining the trade framework. “We took a conscious call to stay out of RCEP because we didn’t think it was going to do any help for us,” she said.
Sitharaman said Indian exporters had turned global trade disruptions into opportunities by identifying alternative markets, including countries that had imposed high tariffs on Indian goods. Exports of goods and services grew 23 per cent in September, she said, citing the performance as evidence of exporters’ resilience amid a difficult global environment.
“Even in this situation Indian exporters have found very many different alternative markets — and even to markets which have literally levied huge tariffs on us — we have reached these markets and very efficiently,” she said.
India remained committed to multilateralism but was accelerating bilateral trade agreements rather than waiting for progress in the global trading system, the minister said. “We believe in multilateralism. However, given today’s environment we are very keen that we build our strength in trade through bilateral agreements as well.”
She cited India’s trade engagements with the European Union, New Zealand, Australia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as negotiations with Canada, saying political will on both sides had helped move long-pending talks forward.
On India-US trade negotiations, following recent comments by Goyal, Sitharaman said: “I hope in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners India and US the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest.”

high_priority_articles.title: Indian Refiners’ Russian Crude Trade Exposes EU Sanctions Gap - Urban Acres
high_priority_articles.summary: Indian Refiners’ Russian Crude Trade Exposes EU Sanctions Gap  Urban Acres
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The figures point to a complex re-routing of energy trade rather than a simple rise in Indian crude consumption. India’s Russian crude imports fell 13 per cent in September, yet refineries operating with Russian feedstock continued to send substantial volumes of fuel to markets in the European Union, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. The central question is therefore not only how much Russian crude India buys, but how sanctions treat products after that crude has passed through a refinery.
The distinction matters because refining transforms the physical product while leaving the commercial and regulatory question of origin contested. The European Union banned imports of oil products refined from Russian crude in January 2026. However, the ban exempts net crude exporters. CREA argues that this exemption leaves a gap because a country’s net-exporter status does not prevent individual refineries within that country from processing Russian-origin crude.
The report recommends applying the restriction at the refinery level. Under that approach, oil products from any plant that had processed Russian crude during the previous six months would be barred, regardless of the declared origin of the specific cargo. This is a recommendation from an advocacy group, not an adopted policy, but it identifies the administrative problem at the heart of the trade: the difficulty of linking a finished fuel cargo to the crude feedstock used months earlier.
India’s refinery network sits at the centre of this issue. Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat supplied six of the seven cargoes unloaded at European Union ports in September, CREA said. The refinery also supplied the group’s largest United States-bound exports, valued at 122 million euros. Russian crude accounted for 32 per cent of Jamnagar’s imports between July and September.
The EU received oil products worth 667 million euros from refineries in India, Turkiye and Brunei that process Russian crude. Australia received products worth 168 million euros, the United States 154 million euros and New Zealand 19 million euros. For the EU-bound shipments, Italy received three of the seven cargoes, Romania received two, and Spain and Cyprus received one each.
The value of exports destined for EU ports from refineries running on Russian crude rose 80 per cent, according to CREA. That figure included a 104,000-tonne gasoil cargo from Jamnagar that was still travelling to Rotterdam. The cargo illustrates the way sanctions enforcement must operate across multiple points: the refinery, the shipping route, the declared destination and the rules governing the receiving market.
At the same time, the volume of Russian crude entering India declined. CREA said imports fell for the second consecutive month and reached their lowest level since April. Intake dropped at India’s three largest Russian-crude-importing refineries: Jamnagar by 27 per cent, Indian Oil Corporation’s Paradip refinery by 21 per cent and Nayara Energy’s Vadinar refinery by 8 per cent.
Vadinar nevertheless overtook Jamnagar as India’s largest importer of Russian crude in September. The change shows why monthly national import figures do not fully explain how the market is being reorganised. A decline in total imports can coexist with shifts between individual facilities, changing cargo flows and continued exports of refined products to sanctioning countries.
Smaller installations also mostly reduced their intake. The HMEL Mundra Oil Terminal cut imports by 74 per cent month on month, while the Kochi refinery reduced them by 32 per cent. The main exception was Indian Oil Corporation’s Mundra Oil Terminal, which received 570,000 tonnes of Russian crude in September after receiving none in August.
India remained Russia’s second-largest fossil-fuel customer in September, buying 4.1 billion euros of Russian hydrocarbons, CREA said. Crude oil accounted for 88 per cent of that total, at 3.6 billion euros. Coal accounted for 309 million euros and oil products for 161 million euros. Only China bought more Russian fossil fuels during the month.
Since December 2022, India has taken 37 per cent of Russia’s crude exports, compared with China’s 50 per cent, according to the report. Before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India was a marginal buyer of Russian oil. Its position changed after Western buyers retreated and Russian crude became available at steep discounts.
The price difference remains an important part of the trade’s economics. Urals crude averaged 90.7 US dollars a barrel in September but remained 23 dollars below Brent, unchanged from August. The discount creates an incentive for refiners to continue assessing Russian crude as part of their feedstock mix, even as the compliance environment becomes more restrictive in some markets.
Kpler analysts attributed part of the September fall in Indian volumes to tighter supply and stronger Chinese competition for Russian barrels, rather than only to pressure from the United States. They expect India’s October imports to remain between 1.8 million and 1.9 million barrels per day. That estimate, as reported in the source material, indicates that India’s role in the trade is not disappearing even if the composition and distribution of imports are changing.
The institutional challenge is that sanctions are being applied to a supply chain that is organised across jurisdictions. Russian crude may be purchased by an Indian refinery, converted into diesel or another petroleum product, and shipped to a market where imports of products made from Russian crude are restricted. Each transaction can have a different legal and commercial identity, while the physical transformation makes the original feedstock less visible in the final cargo.
That creates a governance problem for regulators and customs authorities. A rule based only on the declared origin of a finished product may not capture the origin of the crude used to make it. A refinery-level rule, such as the one proposed by CREA, would make the plant’s recent processing history a central compliance factor. It could also make enforcement more administratively demanding because authorities would need reliable records of crude intake and a defined look-back period.
The available evidence does not establish that the EU or other sanctioning countries have adopted CREA’s recommendation. Nor does it show that any specific cargo breached a final legal determination. What it does establish is a sharp increase in the value of oil products shipped by refineries processing Russian crude, alongside continued imports of Russian hydrocarbons by India and a policy debate over how refined-product restrictions should be enforced.
For Indian cities and the wider built environment, the issue is indirect but important. Refineries are major industrial infrastructure nodes whose operations connect ports, storage terminals, pipelines, shipping routes, manufacturing activity and public revenues. Changes in the source and price of crude can affect how these assets are used, while changes in sanctions rules can alter cargo destinations and the commercial value of refinery capacity.
The September data also show why energy infrastructure cannot be understood only through national import totals. Jamnagar, Vadinar, Paradip, Mundra and Kochi recorded different movements in Russian-crude intake. Those facility-level changes shape port utilisation, tanker movements, storage demand and the export profile of refined products. The distribution of activity across refineries is therefore as significant as the headline decline in India’s total imports.
The evidence points to a market balancing three forces: discounted Russian supply, competition from China for available barrels and growing scrutiny from sanctioning countries. India’s crude imports from Russia declined in September, but the country remained the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels and Indian refineries continued to supply major Western markets.
The next stage of the story will depend on whether sanctioning jurisdictions retain country-level exemptions or move towards refinery-level restrictions. It will also depend on how Indian refiners adjust their crude mix, how Russian supplies are allocated between Indian and Chinese buyers, and whether October imports remain within the 1.8 million-to-1.9 million barrels-per-day range cited by Kpler analysts. The immediate evidence confirms a continuing trade relationship; the unresolved issue is how effectively existing rules can follow crude through the refinery and into the final fuel market.

South Korea plans to relocate a military airfield in Gwangju, where it intends to develop a major semiconductor cluster. The freed-up area of 8.2 square kilometers is to become the central element of 800 trillion won in investment in four chip manufacturing plants by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, The Japan Times reports.
The project is part of President Lee Jae Myung's large-scale program, which provides for investments of 1,350 trillion won, or about $1 trillion, in semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence and data centers. The authorities aim to turn the southwestern Honam region into a technology hub. Last year, its economy contracted by 0.9%, while the country's economy grew by 1.1%.
Relocation of the airfield
The military facility in Gwangju is located about 266 kilometers from Seoul. Part of the territory is reserved for use by the U.S. military in the event of an emergency, so the relocation requires coordination with the United States. About 28,000 U.S. military personnel are stationed in South Korea, and Seoul has not said whether Washington has approved the relocation of the relevant facilities.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Previously, the government planned to relocate or temporarily disperse military facilities by mid-2028. The president instructed officials to consider the possibility of accelerating this process. Under the government's plan, the first of the four factories is to begin mass production by 2030.
U.S. pressure and infrastructure challenges
The plan could become another source of tension in relations with Washington. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Bloomberg Television that South Korea's expansion of its artificial intelligence sector should take place more in the United States and warned of the possibility of new tariffs.
After construction, the factories will need about 650,000 tonnes of water per day. The government expects to use water from nearby reservoirs and treated wastewater, although the region recently experienced a severe drought. The cluster is also expected to require new power transmission lines and about 23,000 workers. South Jeolla Province produces about twice as much electricity as it consumes, but the construction of new energy infrastructure has already sparked protests in rural communities.

high_priority_articles.title: The EU AI Act and UK AI regulation: A product law perspective - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
high_priority_articles.summary: The EU AI Act and UK AI regulation: A product law perspective  Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Don't just teach AI, use it
Regulation EU 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act) is widely regarded as a landmark piece of legislation. It introduces a dedicated legal framework for artificial intelligence (AI), adopts a risk-based approach to regulation, and places fundamental rights considerations at the heart of compliance.
While the EU has adopted a dedicated legislative framework for AI, the UK has, to date, favoured a more principles-based and sector-led approach, relying largely on existing regulatory frameworks. At first glance, that divergence may suggest that the compliance challenges facing businesses operating in the EU and UK are materially different.
For product lawyers, however, many of the concepts underpinning the EU AI Act are not entirely new. Many of its operational requirements, including risk management, post-market monitoring, incident investigation, regulatory notification, and corrective action, reflect concepts that have long featured in product regulation.
For decades, EU product laws have required manufacturers and other economic operators to monitor products through their lifecycle, assess risks, and take appropriate action where issues emerge. Viewed through that lens, many of the EU AI Act's operational requirements, which appear to borrow directly from the product safety playbook, will be familiar to organisations accustomed to product regulatory compliance.
A familiar approach to managing risk
One of the clearest parallels is that compliance obligations do not simply end once a product or system reaches the market.
Under EU product legislation, manufacturers are expected to continue monitoring products, gather information about real-world performance and respond when risks emerge. Increasingly, EU product regulation is built around lifecycle compliance rather than a one-off assessment undertaken before a product is placed on the market. This broader shift towards lifecycle regulation will be familiar to many businesses operating across both EU and UK product regulatory landscapes.
The EU AI Act adopts a similar philosophy. Providers of high-risk AI systems must establish post-market monitoring systems, collect information about the operation of their systems in practice and assess whether risks, incidents or non-conformities emerge after deployment. The objective is not simply to demonstrate compliance before a system reaches the market, but to continually assess whether that system continues to operate as intended.
Responding to risks and non-compliance
The similarities become even clearer when issues arise after products or systems have been placed on the market.
Under Regulation (EU) 2023/988 (the EU General Product Safety Regulation or EU GPSR), a manufacturer that considers, or has reason to believe, that a product is dangerous must act immediately. Depending on the circumstances, this may involve taking corrective measures, including withdrawal, or recall. Authorities must be notified and, where a recall is undertaken, consumers may also need to be informed.
Similar concepts can be found across the broader EU product regulatory framework. For example, under Directive 2011/65/EU (the Restriction on Hazardous Materials Directive or RoHS Directive), manufacturers that consider, or have reason to believe, that an in-scope product is non-compliant must take corrective measures and notify competent authorities.
The EU AI Act adopts both of these approaches:
- Where a provider considers, or has reason to believe, that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity, it must immediately take the necessary corrective action, which may involve bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it.
- Where a provider becomes aware that a high-risk AI system presents a risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights, it must immediately investigate the causes of the risk and inform market surveillance authorities (and, where applicable, the notified body) of the nature of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken.
Incident reporting: product safety thinking applied to AI
The parallels become even more apparent in the EU AI Act's serious incident reporting regime.
Providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to market surveillance authorities. Reports must generally be submitted immediately after the provider establishes, or reasonably suspects, a causal link between the AI system and the incident, and, in any event, no later than 15 days after becoming aware of the incident.
The regime also includes accelerated reporting deadlines in particularly serious circumstances:
- Widespread infringements, or incidents involving serious and irreversible disruption to critical infrastructure, must be reported immediately, and no later than 2 days after the provider (or deployer) becomes aware of that incident.
- Incidents involving death must be reported immediately after a causal relationship is established or suspected and, in any event, no later than 10 days after the provider (or deployer) becomes aware of the incident.
Reporting is only one element of the process. Following the report, providers of high-risk AI systems must also investigate the incident, conduct a risk assessment, cooperate with authorities, and implement any necessary corrective measures.
For organisations with established product safety procedures, many of these requirements will already be well understood. The practical questions are often the same: what happened, is there a causal link, how serious is the risk, does the regulator need to be informed and what corrective action is required?
Although these are classic product safety questions, they are increasingly becoming AI governance questions.
Fundamental rights: the key differentiator
However, there is one important difference.
Traditionally, product safety law has focused on protecting consumers against physical harms such as injury, death, or property damage.
The EU AI Act adopts a broader concept of risk. A serious incident may involve not only health and safety impacts, but also infringements of fundamental rights protected under EU law. For example, risks relating to discrimination, privacy, or freedom of expression may arise even where no physical harm occurs.
In that sense, the EU AI Act expands the categories of harms that must be monitored and managed. This means that, while many of the governance mechanisms found in the EU AI Act resemble those found elsewhere in product regulation, the nature of the risks that need to be assessed is considerably broader.
What about the UK?
Although the UK has not adopted legislation equivalent to the EU AI Act, many of the same governance themes are beginning to emerge through existing regulatory frameworks and guidance. AI-related risks are increasingly being considered through the lens of established product safety, consumer protection, data protection and sector-specific regulation.
For example, organisations developing or deploying AI systems may already need to address AI-related risks under existing UK data protection requirements, while AI-enabled products remain subject to established product safety obligations.
For businesses operating across both jurisdictions, the EU AI Act may therefore have an influence extending beyond those activities that fall directly within its scope. The practical disciplines that it requires, including risk assessment, incident escalation, monitoring and governance, are likely to shape wider organisational practices, even where equivalent legal obligations do not currently exist under a standalone UK AI regime.
What does this mean for businesses?
The practical implication is that compliance with the EU AI Act may not require an entirely new approach to governance.
Many businesses already have established processes for monitoring products, investigating issues and engaging with regulators. For those organisations, the challenge may be less about building entirely new compliance structures and more about adapting existing governance frameworks to address AI-specific risks, including risks relating to fundamental rights.
This may be particularly true for businesses operating across both the UK and EU. Even where organisations are not subject to an equivalent standalone AI regime in the UK, compliance with the EU AI Act may influence governance standards across wider business operations.
Ultimately, while the EU AI Act introduces a novel regulatory framework for AI, businesses that already understand post-market monitoring, incident reporting, corrective action and regulatory engagement may be better placed than they expect to respond to its requirements. The challenge is likely to lie not in the underlying governance disciplines themselves, but in applying them to a new category of risks, including those relating to fundamental rights.

high_priority_articles.title: Political instability is driving Bangladesh's economic collapse - India Today
high_priority_articles.summary: Political instability is driving Bangladesh's economic collapse  India Today
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Bangladesh's prolonged political uncertainty is taking a growing toll on its economy, as businesses hesitate to invest and ordinary households struggle with rising costs. With poverty increasing, job creation stagnating and purchasing power shrinking, the crisis extends beyond inflation and global oil prices.
The rising cost of living in Bangladesh is no longer merely a matter of market prices. Its effects have eroded people's real incomes. As a result, they must continually cut back on everyday expenses.
Recent research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) shows that sharp increases in food and energy prices do not merely generate temporary inflation; the effects of such inflationary crises weigh on a country and its state institutions for a long time. These effects will be prolonged in Bangladesh, too. Poverty has already increased. Many people have fallen below the poverty line. At the same time, employment is contracting and production is declining, and the situation is worsening by the day. The gap between the economically privileged and the disadvantaged is set to widen considerably.
A recent Reuters report on poverty said a new IMF economic model calculated the disproportionately greater impact of inflation on poor households. According to the model, between 2021 and 2024, about 23 million more people fell into extreme poverty than previous estimates indicated. The IMF will publish the research as a chapter in its forthcoming World Economic Outlook.
This warning is particularly important for Bangladesh, because the figures being presented to show that inflation is declining conceal a mathematical sleight of hand. The reported decline in inflation uses 2025 as the comparison year, measuring the current rate against that year's abnormally high inflation. Meanwhile, the IMF model discussed in the Reuters report was developed with politically stable countries in mind. And in those countries, rising energy prices have been treated as the principal cause of inflation.
But in countries such as Bangladesh, Afghanistan, and Myanmar, rising energy prices are not the sole underlying cause of inflation. Moreover, inflation had already become acute in Afghanistan, Myanmar, and Bangladesh before the outbreak of the war between America and Iran.
In Bangladesh, inflation reached alarming levels immediately after Yunus illegally seized power. After Yunus left power, oil prices rose as a consequence of the US-Iran war. In reality, the main reason for inflation in countries like these is that state structures have been dismantled. In Afghanistan, Taliban militants dismantled those structures. In Myanmar, they were broken down through armed rebellions by various ethnic groups and the military’s overthrow of the elected government.
In Bangladesh, too, an NGO figure named Yunus dismantled the structures of the state by bringing together militants and various groups to overthrow a stable government through "meticulous design". Several religious-nationalist political parties helped Yunus dismantle those structures and create anarchy in the country. The starkest example of the dismantling of state structures in Bangladesh is the enactment of a law to protect the killers of police officers instead of bringing them to justice. Judges were even forced to resign through mob violence at the Supreme Court.
Meanwhile, as in Myanmar, a so-called elected government has been formed in Bangladesh under the guise of an election in which only one political grouping participated. Since the election did not reflect public opinion, political stability has, naturally, not followed. Consequently, as in Afghanistan and Myanmar, political instability is the principal reason Bangladesh is being drawn ever further into poverty.
Beyond the parameters of the IMF model, Bangladesh stands alongside Afghanistan and Myanmar in Asia as a country experiencing a more severe rise in poverty and inflation. Here, poverty and inflation will not merely decline slowly; the situation may instead descend into an even deeper crisis.
When energy prices rise and global trade, including the energy trade, shifts onto new paths, every country must confront changing circumstances with considerable caution and competence. Governing at such a time demands a much higher level of capability. Above all, it requires national unity, a stable country, and leadership that commands trust.
At present, as in Myanmar, the activities of Bangladesh's principal political party are banned. The leader of Bangladesh's principal party, the Awami League, is currently in India as a state guest. She has announced through the international media that she will return to the country in December. From this, observers at home and abroad understand that the country is about to enter a new political chapter.
Naturally, therefore, domestic and foreign businesspeople want to get through this period without taking risks. This reluctance among businesspeople to act is pushing Bangladesh further into economic stagnation with every passing day.
The damage Yunus, the NGO leader who seized power, inflicted on the country's military and civilian structures and its economic sector presents the greatest obstacle this government faces in trying to overcome the crisis. In most areas, this government continues to follow Yunus's policies. As a result, it has essentially defined itself as Yunus 2.0. It was not properly elected, with actual participation in the election amounting to only 12% to 15% of voters.
For this reason, rising inflation and poverty in Bangladesh cannot be attributed solely to higher energy prices. Far more consequential are political instability, the government's lack of popular representation, the absence of capable state leadership, and the lack of a clear direction for governing the country.
FROM YUNUS TO THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT: INFLATION REMAINS HIGH
The World Bank's April 2026 Bangladesh Development Update raised similar concerns. The institution reported inflation at around 8.5 percent in the 2026 fiscal year, with prices remaining high for both food and non-food items. As low-income workers' wages failed to keep pace with prices, their purchasing power declined.
In its July 2026 forecast, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) projected inflation in Bangladesh at 9% for 2026 and 8.8% for 2027. It raised its 2027 inflation forecast because it feared the second-round effects of energy and electricity costs would persist.
The IMF's revised October forecast paints a more troubling picture, putting GDP growth at 3.2% and inflation above 10%. The modest easing anticipated in July has thus given way to a forecast of renewed inflationary pressure alongside weak economic growth.
Since July, however, global politics, oil prices, and oil supply routes have become increasingly complicated. A new chapter in the US-Iran war began in September. In this chapter, the Houthis have put another oil transport route, the Red Sea, at risk; by attacking a Saudi airport in October, they have placed Saudi airspace in the same predicament.
As a result, the political and security situation has already become more complicated not only in the Middle East but also in Pakistan. If Pakistan commits itself more deeply to the Mecca agreement, it will find itself in still greater difficulty. Following the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, analysts in Pakistan are saying that the country's political, security, and energy crises will all intensify. Entering a framework such as the Mecca agreement bears much of the responsibility for this predicament.
Bangladesh, meanwhile, has already become more deeply entangled in its relationship with Pakistan. It has expressed a desire to join the Mecca Pact. Bangladesh may therefore have to bear some of the consequences that fall on Pakistan. The more actively Pakistan involves itself in Saudi Arabia, the more it will expose itself as a target for the Houthis and Iran. If Bangladesh continues to support Pakistan openly in this manner at such a time, its energy import routes may face disruption.
In both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, the countries of the Mecca Pact and their supporters will face obstruction as part of Iran's and the Houthis' war effort. With its present instability and weak economy, Bangladesh will find it extremely difficult to withstand the pressures of such a situation. The country's stability and international position will become even more precarious.
Above all, with the war entering this new chapter, any assurance that global oil prices will fall has become increasingly implausible. The cost of transporting oil, which stood at $30,000, has now reached $1.2 million. At this moment, the world sees no prospect of that cost falling; it sees only further increases.
It is therefore impossible to reduce inflation or prevent poverty from rising merely by controlling oil prices or thinking in terms of oil alone. What Bangladesh needs first and foremost is capable political leadership to govern the country. From the New Deal to the recovery from recession during Obama's presidency, political decisions shaped the way out of economic crisis.
Economic conditions and available resources alone were not the determining factor. Again, although widely condemned in history, Adolf Hitler brought about economic development in his country after World War l through political decisions, as did Japan's leadership after World War ll.
Even in Bangladesh, when the Awami League-led Grand Alliance formed the government in 2009, the country was facing a severe energy crisis. The world was in recession. The government at the time overcame these difficulties by using political decisions to guide the economy and make energy policy an integral part of it. To overcome the recession, the government set energy production targets, took swift decisions, and began work, despite condemnation from many quarters.
It focused on restoring economic momentum by increasing purchasing power in the domestic marke

high_priority_articles.title: China imposes export curbs on tunnel boring machines, raising concerns for India’s infrastructure projects - Business Upturn
high_priority_articles.summary: China imposes export curbs on tunnel boring machines, raising concerns for India’s infrastructure projects  Business Upturn
high_priority_articles.full_text:
China’s Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs have announced export controls on tunnel boring machines and related components, alongside restrictions covering specialised excavators and high-altitude concrete-spraying equipment. The measures, announced on Monday, will take effect on November 18 and could complicate procurement for infrastructure projects that rely on Chinese-made machinery. Beijing says the controls are intended to protect national security and national interests.
The move is relevant to India, where tunnel boring machines are used to construct underground metro corridors, railway tunnels and road links through difficult terrain. However, China’s announcement does not specifically name India or establish that any particular Indian project will be delayed. The impact will depend on the equipment involved, applicable licensing requirements and whether alternative suppliers can meet project needs.
The new controls cover full-section tunnel boring machines, including earth-pressure-balance and rock-tunnelling machines, as well as purpose-built components such as cutterheads, screw conveyors, segment erectors and main drive systems. Certain walking excavators and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines are also included. The latter equipment is designed for high-altitude construction, where concrete mixtures must be pumped and sprayed onto working surfaces.
China’s notice sets out different compliance requirements depending on the destination and item. Exports of specified controlled equipment to sensitive countries and regions with which China has disputes require licences. For other destinations, the announcement provides for registration and declarations, alongside undertakings against unauthorised onward transfers to sensitive destinations. Exporters must identify controlled goods accurately in customs declarations, while shipments may be held if authorities question the information supplied.
The announcement also adjusts controls on selected dredging equipment, including slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads that meet specified technical thresholds. These items are used to remove underwater sediment during harbour, river and marine construction.
The development comes amid previous concerns over access to tunnelling equipment manufactured in China. In 2024, Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal raised the issue of a German manufacturer facing difficulties exporting tunnel boring machines from China to India, according to contemporary media reports. The latest announcement formalises controls for specified equipment but does not, by itself, confirm a blanket ban on supplies to India.
China’s commerce ministry said qualifying export licence applications would be reviewed under its laws and approved when requirements are met. The next key date is November 18, when the measures take effect. Indian infrastructure developers and equipment suppliers will need to assess sourcing arrangements and possible delivery risks as implementation details emerge.

high_priority_articles.title: China tightens export curbs on TBM raising fresh concerns over India’s infrastructure projects - PSU Watch
high_priority_articles.summary: China tightens export curbs on TBM raising fresh concerns over India’s infrastructure projects  PSU Watch
high_priority_articles.full_text:
New Delhi: China has announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel boring machines (TBMs) and other specialised heavy equipment, raising fresh concerns over India’s dependence on Chinese machinery for critical infrastructure projects, including metro networks, high-speed rail corridors and strategically important tunnels near border areas.
The restrictions, announced by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Monday, will come into effect on November 18. Beijing has justified the move on grounds of national security and protection of its strategic interests.
However, the decision raises uncomfortable questions for India, which continues to depend on foreign suppliers for several categories of sophisticated infrastructure equipment despite its ambitious push for domestic manufacturing under the Make in India initiative.
India’s infrastructure ambitions face fresh uncertainty
Tunnel boring machines are critical to the construction of underground metro corridors, railway tunnels and other major infrastructure projects. Any disruption in their availability could affect project schedules, increase procurement costs and complicate the execution of ongoing and proposed projects.
The latest restrictions are particularly significant because China has previously obstructed the supply of TBMs to India.
In 2024, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal raised the issue with German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, pointing out that Beijing was preventing a German company manufacturing tunnel boring machines in China from exporting them to India.
The episode exposed a major vulnerability in India’s infrastructure supply chain: even machinery supplied by European companies can become subject to Chinese restrictions when manufacturing facilities are located in China.
The latest controls could deepen that vulnerability, although their actual impact will depend on licensing decisions, the equipment covered and the availability of alternative suppliers.
Strategic implications for border infrastructure
The restrictions extend beyond conventional tunnelling machinery to include walking excavators and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines, both used in difficult terrain.
Walking excavators are designed to operate on steep, uneven and otherwise inaccessible surfaces, while plateau-type wet shotcrete machines are used for concrete spraying operations in high-altitude environments.
These machines can be important for infrastructure construction in mountainous regions, including areas along India’s sensitive northern borders.
The decision therefore raises strategic concerns at a time when India is expanding road, rail and tunnel connectivity in difficult Himalayan terrain.
While China has not explicitly identified India as a target of the latest measures, the restrictions demonstrate how control over specialised machinery can potentially become an instrument of geopolitical leverage.
Beijing has also tightened export controls on specified dredging equipment, including slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads.
The restrictions cover slurry pumps with inlet diameters of at least 0.55 metres and maximum rotational speeds of 400 revolutions per minute, along with certain large pump casings and impellers.
Controls will also apply to dragheads used in trailing suction hopper dredgers and cutterheads deployed in cutter suction dredgers that meet specified technical thresholds.
Such equipment is important for port development, harbour maintenance, maritime infrastructure and underwater excavation.
For India, which is pursuing major port expansion and maritime connectivity programmes, restrictions on specialised dredging components could introduce another layer of supply-chain uncertainty.
The latest announcement follows a draft proposal released by MOFCOM on Friday seeking additional export restrictions on 14 technologies across sectors including artificial intelligence, biotechnology and photovoltaic solar power.
Together, these measures point to China’s increasing use of export controls over advanced technologies and specialised industrial equipment.
Under the new rules, exporters must obtain licences from MOFCOM under China’s Export Control Law and regulations governing dual-use items.
Exporters will also have to declare the relevant control codes and provide detailed technical specifications. Chinese customs authorities can hold shipments pending verification of the information submitted.
This licensing framework gives Beijing greater oversight of sensitive equipment exports and could create uncertainty for overseas buyers even where shipments are not explicitly prohibited.
China’s latest move should serve as a warning for India’s infrastructure planners and policymakers.
India has committed substantial public investment to expanding highways, railways, metro networks, ports and strategic border connectivity. Yet dependence on imported specialised machinery remains a potential weakness in the execution of these projects.
The bigger question is whether India’s domestic manufacturing ecosystem has developed the technological capabilities needed to reduce this dependence.
An export licensing requirement is not the same as an outright export ban. Nevertheless, China’s ability to delay, scrutinise or deny shipments of critical machinery highlights the risks of concentrated supply chains.
For New Delhi, the challenge is no longer limited to securing alternative suppliers. It must also accelerate domestic design, manufacturing and servicing capabilities for advanced tunnelling, excavation and dredging equipment.
Otherwise, India’s ambitious infrastructure expansion could remain vulnerable to decisions taken in Beijing.
The larger concern is straightforward: Can India claim strategic infrastructure independence when access to some of the machines needed to build that infrastructure remains subject to another country’s export approvals?
