high_priority_articles.title: How could Israel most effectively support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis? - The Jerusalem Post
high_priority_articles.summary: How could Israel most effectively support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis?  The Jerusalem Post
high_priority_articles.full_text:
There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. How might such help take shape, and what might be most effective?
This comes amid wider questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have come up since the accords began in 2020. So far, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.
Now, US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments were made days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.
The context for this latest development is the Houthis’ increased attacks on Saudi Arabia. America has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence.
The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.
On Sunday, Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg.
“Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. The security establishment is aware that there is an opportunity to strengthen relations, but is not addressing the issue for fear of inflaming the situation,” Bohbot reported.
The Turkish pro-government media outlet Anadolu Agency noted on October 13 that “Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen’s Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh’s approval through US mediation.”
Anadolu Agency said it based this on a report in Haaretz. “Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement,” the report said. “There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.”
Saudi Arabia needs Israeli aerial defense systems
Ynet noted on Sunday, in a piece by Ron Ben-Yishai, that “the Saudis urgently need early-warning radar systems and air defense batteries capable of countering different types of aerial threats, including Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and even Arrow 2 interceptors.”
“The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and explosive-laden drones, requiring a combination of defensive capabilities,” he added.
This analysis noted that “Trump sees a chance to revive Saudi-Israel normalization as the Houthis strike Riyadh; Israel is sharing intelligence, but Riyadh’s demand for Palestinian statehood talks and Israel’s need for its own defenses make a deal far from certain.”
It also added that Trump may see an “opportunity for greater Israeli assistance, potentially generating enough goodwill in Riyadh to persuade the Saudis to abandon their longstanding condition for normalization: negotiations with the Palestinians toward a two-state solution. For now, however, there is good reason to doubt that Trump’s comments signal a meaningful breakthrough in Israeli-Saudi relations.”
Walla noted that “security sources confirmed that as time goes by, the contribution of Israeli intelligence is increasing, with the Houthis in the background causing heavy damage to the Saudis throughout the country.”
The report goes on to say that “as first published in Walla, the IDF is assisting Saudi Arabia on the intelligence front in the fight against the Houthis in aspects of warning, target banking, and building a situational picture.”
“Israel sees this as a positive process that will intensify once the US decides how it will decide on the Iranian issue,” it said.
America, Walla said, is facing this dilemma: “If the US attacks Iran, the latter may attack the countries of the region, including Israel. If America continues with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), this could also lead to escalation in the region.”
Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7
The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It’s worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel.
The Iranian-backed group said that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.
One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea.
Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. A Japanese company operated the vessel and, through its ownership structure, was linked to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.
The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This shows that Israel has already launched a campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.
Notably, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis.
It appears that Riyadh will work again with Egypt and the UAE. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with the US Central Command.
Any cooperation against the Houthis can strengthen regional defense ties and infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran’s direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

high_priority_articles.title: UK publishes CBAM default emissions values ahead of 2027 launch - edie
high_priority_articles.summary: UK publishes CBAM default emissions values ahead of 2027 launch  edie
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Published by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) today (19 October), the values cover aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel.
The mechanism is intended to address carbon leakage, which occurs when production moves to countries with weaker climate policies or lower carbon costs.
UK CBAM will apply to imports of covered goods, with the tax calculated by reference to the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions generated during their production, subject to relevant carbon pricing adjustments.
The Emissions and Verification Regulations establish how embodied emissions must be calculated, how the underlying data must be monitored and verified, and which records businesses must retain.
Importers can use one of two methods to calculate emissions. The first is to apply the published default value for the relevant CBAM good. The calculation involves multiplying the weight of the imported goods by the applicable emissions value, without requiring independent verification of the emissions figure.
The alternative is to use actual emissions data from the installation where the goods were manufactured or processed. This method requires more detailed information and independent verification by accredited third-party verifiers, but may result in a lower calculated emissions figure and, consequently, a lower tax liability.
Importers bringing in less than £10,000 worth of covered CBAM goods over a 12-month period are exempt from registration and reporting obligations.
Transitional period to allow accounting flexibility
The UK CBAM is scheduled to begin on 1 January 2027. A transitional period will run from 1 January 2027 to 30 June 2028, allowing businesses flexibility around accounting periods and initial payments before full quarterly reporting and tax liabilities take effect.
The launch will coincide with the second allocation phase of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS), covering 2027 to 2030. During this period, free emissions allowances for domestic producers will be phased out over several years, with the aim of maintaining parity between UK production and imports subject to CBAM.
Six-year record-keeping requirement
HMRC has also published guidance on the records businesses must retain under the mechanism.
CBAM records must be kept in written form, including electronically, for six years from the later of the date the records were created or the end of the accounting period to which they relate.
Businesses that fail to retain the required records may face a fixed penalty of £500. Separate penalties may apply if an importer fails to provide information or documents when requested by HMRC.
The requirements mean importers will need to maintain records supporting their emissions calculations and compliance with the scheme, whether they use default values or actual emissions data.
The UK mechanism follows the same broad approach as the EU’s CBAM, although the UK is developing its own rules and administrative requirements.
The EU’s definitive CBAM phase began in 2026, increasing the focus on carbon costs across international industrial supply chains.
The UK scheme’s introduction in 2027 will add another set of carbon reporting and tax requirements for businesses importing covered industrial goods into the country.

high_priority_articles.title: Armenia–Russia Relations: Toward Confrontation or Dialogue? - MassisPost
high_priority_articles.summary: Armenia–Russia Relations: Toward Confrontation or Dialogue?  MassisPost
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By KRIKOR KHODANIAN
Relations between the Republic of Armenia and the Russian Federation have entered a difficult and tense period. The two countries, once allies, are now deeply divided over how to reassess the past and shape their future relationship.
The 44-day war and the events that followed—particularly Russia’s indifference when Azerbaijani forces invaded Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2022, followed by its abandonment of the Armenians of Artsakh, whom it had been entrusted to protect—have left Armenians deeply disillusioned. This disappointment will be difficult to overcome in the foreseeable future.
Yerevan is seeking to redefine its future relations with Moscow on a new basis, with Armenia’s national and state interests serving as the guiding principles. Moscow, however, maintains that the former ties should be restored and that the two countries should remain loyal allies and partners in all fields, including the economy, politics, defense, and other areas.
Senior Russian officials continue to oppose Armenia’s foreign policy of closer ties with European countries, issuing warnings at times and threats at others. Among the latest was a statement by Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s former president and current deputy chairman of its Security Council, who warned that Armenia could become “the new Ukraine.”
“Armenia’s current leadership has decided to change the direction of its development. I am confident that this will lead to nothing good. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is its transformation into a new Ukraine,” he said.
Since the war in Ukraine began, Medvedev has effectively been tasked with delivering some of the most extreme statements directed against the West. He has repeatedly threatened the use of nuclear weapons as a means of bringing the war to an end. His latest remarks directed at Armenia should therefore be viewed in this broader context.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described Medvedev’s comments as incomprehensible, adding:
“Armenia has already faced such a danger and found itself in a similar situation when the CSTO failed to fulfill its obligations toward Armenia. Why is Mr. Medvedev making such a statement? One could just as easily make a statement warning that Armenia might suddenly turn into a new Russia, given that explosions are occurring in various parts of Russia. This is not a good genre.”
Despite the accusations coming from the Kremlin, Yerevan is trying to avoid a complete rupture in relations with Moscow, seeking to resolve existing disagreements on the basis of mutual respect.
Thanks to these efforts, contacts between the leaders of the two countries, which had been interrupted for a period following Armenia’s parliamentary elections, have resumed. Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Vladimir Putin have held several bilateral meetings and telephone conversations on the sidelines of international summits, seeking common ground on outstanding issues.
Until recently, Pashinyan had stated that Armenia needed small modular nuclear power plants that could be built by American companies. He has since changed his position, arguing that the construction of a large nuclear power plant would be more appropriate, while leaving open the possibility of entrusting the project to Russian companies. In this way, Yerevan appears to be signaling that it is not constrained by its differences with Moscow and remains willing to continue cooperating with Russia.
Several outstanding issues remain to be resolved, the most important of which concerns the management of Armenia’s railway network. Yerevan believes that control of the network should be transferred from the Russian company currently operating it to a company from another country, allowing Armenia’s railways to connect with regional transportation networks. Otherwise, Armenia risks being excluded from new projects because of the sanctions imposed on Russian companies.
Moscow firmly rejects this proposal. Is Yerevan raising the possibility of entrusting the construction of a nuclear power plant to Russian companies in an attempt to soften Moscow’s position on railway management? The answer may become clear in the coming months.
Negotiations on gas supplies are also expected in December. During these talks, Russia may demand a price increase, arguing that Armenia currently benefits from discounted gas prices as a member of the Eurasian Economic Union. However, if Armenia has chosen the path toward European Union membership, Russia may argue that it should pay international market prices, which are several times higher.
Russia has recently unveiled a new initiative dubbed the “Putin Route.” The project aims to connect Russia, Georgia, and Armenia through the construction of roads and railways running through Abkhazia. The initiative is viewed as a geopolitical response to the “Trump Route,” which passes through Armenia and has already begun moving toward implementation.
Armenia–Russia relations thus face new tests and challenges that must be addressed with composure and pragmatism. At every turn, Armenia has demonstrated its willingness to engage in sincere and constructive dialogue. The remaining question is whether the Russian side will demonstrate the same willingness.

How Taiwan's New AI Chip Export Controls Could Affect China
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan is preparing to impose stricter export controls on advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers destined for China, a move that could significantly change how the island regulates the international trade of high-performance computing equipment.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed in an October 12 interview with Bloomberg that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its list of controlled export items.
Under the proposed framework, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization could become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
The government has not announced when the new restrictions will take effect.
The proposal represents a potentially significant development for Taiwan, which occupies a central position in the global AI hardware supply chain.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) manufactures advanced chips used by leading technology companies, while Taiwanese manufacturers play a major role in assembling AI servers for international customers.
The new restrictions could therefore affect not only chip shipments but also the movement of complete computing systems.
What AI chip export restrictions does Taiwan already have?
Taiwan already operates a strategic high-tech export control system, including controls on sensitive technologies and restrictions involving designated entities.
Companies exporting controlled products must comply with applicable licensing requirements and restrictions on prohibited destinations or end users.
Taiwan has also expanded restrictions involving certain Chinese technology companies, including Huawei and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).
However, these existing controls are not identical to the broader restrictions now being proposed.
The central issue is whether Taiwan can more directly regulate shipments of advanced AI hardware to China, including products that may be diverted through intermediaries.
The proposed measures would strengthen the domestic legal framework for controlling certain shipments.
They should not be interpreted as a blanket ban on every semiconductor or server exported to China.
The exact product categories, technical thresholds, licensing exemptions, and enforcement procedures will depend on the final regulations.
What is Taiwan planning to change?
According to Kung, Taiwan intends to add advanced AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled export list.
The measures are intended to align more closely with restrictions imposed by the United States.
Washington has limited China's access to certain advanced AI accelerators and semiconductor technologies on national security grounds.
Taiwan's proposed changes could make it harder for companies to use Taiwanese manufacturing and export channels to circumvent those restrictions.
Crucially, the government is also seeking stronger domestic enforcement powers.
Under the proposed framework, unauthorized exports of newly controlled AI hardware could be prosecuted directly under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
That would differ from situations in which authorities must rely on other existing legal provisions to investigate suspected smuggling or misrepresentation.
However, criminal liability would depend on the final legal framework, the goods involved, and the specific conduct.
Why does the United States want Taiwan to tighten export controls?
The United States has sought to restrict China's access to advanced computing hardware that could support military applications, intelligence operations, and sophisticated artificial intelligence systems.
But export controls become less effective when restricted products can be purchased through intermediaries or redirected through international supply chains.
Taiwan is especially important because of its role in semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly.
Even when a chip is designed by an American company, its production, packaging, integration, or final system assembly may involve Taiwanese businesses.
That creates a need for coordination across jurisdictions.
In his October interview, Kung linked Taiwan's planned adjustments to commitments made under the 2026 US–Taiwan trade agreement.
Closer coordination could reduce differences between the two countries' regulatory systems, although the precise scope of the Taiwanese measures remains to be announced.
How could the restrictions affect Nvidia and Taiwan's AI server manufacturers?
The potential impact depends on the products covered and the destination of shipments.
Nvidia designs AI accelerators that are manufactured through a global supply chain involving TSMC and other partners.
Taiwanese manufacturers also assemble complete servers incorporating these processors.
A restriction covering only certain semiconductor products would have a different effect from one covering finished AI servers.
For example, a complete server may contain multiple accelerators, memory, networking components, and supporting hardware.
Regulating finished systems could reduce opportunities to circumvent chip-specific restrictions by exporting assembled equipment.
Manufacturers would need to evaluate product classifications, customer identities, ultimate end users, and licensing obligations.
However, it would be premature to estimate the financial impact on individual companies before the government publishes the controlled-item definitions.
Why has AI chip smuggling become a major issue?
Advanced AI accelerators are expensive and strategically important products.
Restrictions on their sale to China have created incentives for unauthorized resale, diversion, and complex procurement arrangements.
Authorities in several jurisdictions have investigated suspected attempts to move restricted computing equipment through intermediaries.
For Taiwan, the challenge is particularly sensitive because of the concentration of semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly on the island.
The issue also raises questions about the responsibilities of manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, and overseas customers.
Existing CommonWealth reporting on the Supermicro AI hardware controversy examined how international trade restrictions can intersect with Taiwan's technology supply chains.
The proposed export-control changes would give Taiwanese authorities an additional policy instrument to address such risks.
Could Taiwan's new rules stop China from obtaining advanced AI chips?
Stricter controls could make unauthorized shipments more difficult and increase the legal risks for participants.
However, export restrictions alone cannot guarantee that prohibited hardware will never reach China.
Their effectiveness depends on enforcement, international cooperation, product traceability, and the ability to identify indirect shipments.
The final impact will also depend on whether the new regulations cover individual chips, assembled servers, or both.
For Taiwan, the challenge is to strengthen compliance without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate technology trade.
FAQs
Has Taiwan banned AI chip exports to China?
No blanket ban has been established by the announced proposal. Taiwan already has controls on certain sensitive products and entities, and the government plans to expand restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
When will Taiwan's new AI chip export controls take effect?
As of October 19, 2026, the government has not announced an implementation date.
Which AI chips will be restricted?
The government has indicated that advanced semiconductors and AI servers will be included. Detailed technical specifications and product classifications have not yet been announced.
Will exporting AI chips to China become a criminal offense?
Unauthorized exports of products covered by the proposed new controls could become subject to criminal prosecution under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act once the measures take effect. This does not mean every chip export to China would be illegal.
Will the restrictions affect TSMC?
They could affect compliance requirements for relevant products and transactions involving Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain. The direct implications will depend on the final rules and existing contractual and regulatory arrangements.
Are Taiwan's export controls the same as those of the United States?
No. Taiwan and the United States operate separate legal systems. Taiwan is seeking closer alignment, but companies must evaluate their obligations under each applicable jurisdiction.
The Bottom Line
Taiwan's planned AI export controls are significant because they could close a gap between the island's central role in manufacturing advanced computing hardware and its ability to enforce restrictions on unauthorized shipments.
But the measures remain a proposal until the government publishes and implements the relevant regulations.
For companies operating across Taiwan, China, and the United States, the most important questions are which products will be covered, what licenses will be required, and how the new rules will be enforced.
Policy status: October 19, 2026. The proposed expansion of export controls has been publicly confirmed, but the implementation date and complete product coverage have not been announced.

A viral post says SoftBank's debt is growing fast just as Fed rate hike worries are rising, and traders are asking whether the stress could reach crypto.
We checked each claim against the company's own filings and the Federal Reserve's official pages.
Some numbers hold up well. Others are market prices that no official source can confirm, and we mark them clearly. The original post is linked for reference.
SoftBank's Q1 financial report lists total borrowings of about ¥26.6 trillion at June 30, 2026. That is roughly $164 billion at the quarter-end exchange rate (our conversion), so the headline figure is right.
One detail matters: this covers the whole group, including units like SoftBank Corp. The parent company's own debt is ¥12.2 trillion, or about $75B.
The report links the jump in interest costs to an $11.5B loan backed by Arm shares from December 2025 and $20B drawn from bridge loans in April 2026.
Some loans are also "non-recourse," meaning lenders can claim only the pledged shares, not the parent's other assets.
The report puts roughly ¥5.4 trillion in that group, backed by Arm shares, SoftBank Corp. shares and other holdings.

| New $11B raised at up to 9.75% | Confirmed: about $11.1B, highest 9.75% |

Both S&P and Fitch rate them BB+, one notch below investment grade. They carry no collateral and no guarantee.

On October 1, SoftBank confirmed it paid the third and final $10 billion installment of a $30 billion follow-on investment in OpenAI.

Total invested is now $64.6 billion, for a stake of about 13%. The bond sale paid for this last installment.
The bond sale also closed out a temporary loan. The company's $40 billion bridge loan, signed in March with five banks, was due on March 25, 2027.
Per the October 1 release, all borrowings under it are repaid and the unused $10 billion was cancelled.

high_priority_articles.title: India-US tariff standoff: Why New Delhi must balance trade interests with strategic autonomy | Hindustan Times - Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.summary: India-US tariff standoff: Why New Delhi must balance trade interests with strategic autonomy | Hindustan Times  Hindustan Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
This article is authored by K P Vijayalakshmi.
India and the US face renewed tariff tensions even as strategic cooperation deepened over the last decade. Recurring trade disputes, particularly at times of severe global crises, is a major irritant for both in the management of bilateral as well as global economies. More importantly, economic friction when colliding with geopolitical alignment has renewed the importance of sustained negotiation.
Since 2004, deepening strategic convergence has supported expanding commercial ties despite a persistent US goods deficit. Revised US Census data show that, in July 2025, US goods exports to India were $3.418 billion, while imports were $9.161 billion. Total bilateral trade in goods and services reached $241.66 billion in 2025. At the same time, shared concerns about China strengthened Indo-Pacific cooperation, illustrating how commercial friction and strategic alignment can coincide.
India’s central challenge is to manage persistent trade irritants without compromising its geopolitical interests. This requires focused negotiations, supply-chain diversification, and deeper cooperation in critical sectors such as pharmaceuticals, technology, energy, and defence.
US–India tariff tensions reflect a longstanding divide between India’s development-oriented economic policies and the American preference for freer trade. From the 1950s through the 1980s, India relied on high tariffs, licensing, and import substitution. Washington viewed these measures as trade barriers, while New Delhi defended them as necessary for industrialisation, economic sovereignty, and protection of infant industries.
After the 1991 economic reforms, India progressively lowered barriers and opened its market to US goods. The 2008 civil nuclear agreement accelerated strategic ties, while expanding commerce added economic weight to the partnership.
Deeper engagement, however, did not eliminate trade friction. Disputes and negotiations continued across agriculture, textiles, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, information technology, intellectual property, and industrial goods. Since 2000, many disagreements have entered the WTO framework, showing that growth in commercial ties has not displaced protectionist pressures in either country.
The conflict is more than an economic quarrel. It illustrates differing issues that have produced prolonged negotiations. Both approach it differently: While Washington combines market-access demands with forceful bargaining, India responds through pragmatism, selective resistance, and cooperative signaling. The sharpest escalation came during the first Trump administration.
In 2018, the US imposed national-security tariffs on steel and aluminium, including imports from India. New Delhi retaliated against selected U.S. products, including almonds, apples, and walnuts. In 2019, Washington removed India from the Generalised System of Preferences, ending duty-free access for several Indian exports and intensifying bilateral bargaining.
India has recently agreed to lower or remove tariffs on a variety of US industrial items, agricultural products (including tree nuts, fruits, and soybean oil), and technological products as part of an ongoing interim trade agreement.
Recurring tariff disputes thus test whether both sides can balance commercial interests with their geopolitical partnership and sustain bipartisan support for Indo-US relations in both countries.
Due to recent changes in US trade policy and legal modifications, the US currently imposes a temporary 10% duty on numerous qualified Indian imports. The decrease to 10% came after India changed its foreign trade regulations pertaining to supply chain norms, substituting the high punitive rates associated with former trade and oil disputes.
Current pressures also reflect links between supply-chain shifts, competition with China, energy security, and India’s Russian oil purchases. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed the Senate 86–11 on August 7 and the House 262–159 on September 16. It authorises tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. Although India is not singled out, the measure could constrain its effort to secure affordable supplies.
The US nevertheless remains a major export market and a vital partner in defence, critical technologies, space, education, semiconductors, critical minerals, and Indo-Pacific cooperation. India must therefore protect its export interests while preserving strategic autonomy and preventing trade disputes from weakening the broader relationship.
India has reiterated its obligation to provide 1.4 billion people with energy security. It has promised to safeguard national economic interests in conjunction with industry while informing US interlocutors of the law's potential effects on bilateral relations and international energy markets. While maintaining firmness, this balancing approach should refrain from escalatory rhetoric.
India should refine this approach through five mutually reinforcing measures.
First, pursue targeted negotiations. India should seek product-specific exemptions or lower duties where its exports support US consumers and supply chains. Priorities include textiles, pharmaceuticals, gems and jewellery, leather, marine products, engineering goods, and auto components.
Second, keep retaliation selective. Retaliation may raise input costs, burden consumers, and disrupt US technology, investment, defence, and education links. Tariffs should remain a calibrated negotiating instrument rather than an automatic reaction.
Third, protect vulnerable exporters while improving competitiveness. Labour-intensive and MSME-heavy sectors need time-bound support through faster tax refunds, working-capital assistance, export-credit guarantees, logistics support, and export insurance. Relief should cushion sudden order losses without becoming a permanent subsidy and should accompany reforms in productivity, infrastructure, and standards.
Fourth, diversify markets and deepen political engagement. India should expand trade with the EU, UK, UAE, Australia, Japan, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Simpler rules-of-origin procedures, MSME guidance, export help desks, and quality-certification support would improve use of trade agreements. Additionally, continued engagement with the US Congress, industry, and policy institutions can sustain support for the partnership.
Fifth, expand sectoral cooperation. Pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, critical minerals, clean energy, digital technology, and defence manufacturing offer scope for joint production, trusted supply chains, and regulatory coordination that favour stability over recurring tariff confrontation.
US-India trade friction is longstanding, but commercial trade and investments are embedded in a strategic partnership. India should, therefore, combine negotiation, selective retaliation, exporter support, market diversification, competitive reforms internally while enhancing critical-sector cooperation with strategic partners such as the US. This approach would protect exports while preserving strategic autonomy and the relationship’s value.
(The views expressed are personal)

high_priority_articles.title: Trump's Russia sanctions waiver eases India's energy woes, lifts trade deal chances - A News
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump's Russia sanctions waiver eases India's energy woes, lifts trade deal chances  A News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump's waiver of Russian sanctions eases energy concerns for India, one of the top importers of Russian oil, and may improve the chances of New Delhi and Washington agreeing on a trade deal, besides helping overall ties.
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start this week under the legislation known as the Graham Act.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interest of the United States.
The legislation would have exposed Indian goods to stiff tariffs of up to 100% as India is one of the five largest importers of Russian oil and posed a challenge for the Asian nation's energy policies.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration warned last month the new tariff measures on Russia could hurt bilateral ties, adding to diplomatic strain and trade uncertainty.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrives in India on Tuesday, said trade talks with New Delhi were a consideration for Trump's decision.
"We are trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now and we are very close to doing that. So, that's one of the things we take into consideration when the President makes a decision about national security waivers," Rubio told reporters in Uzbekistan on Monday.
India is the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer. Earlier this year, Russia accounted for nearly half of the country's oil imports, but purchases fell in August and continue to decline.
Persistently cutting Russian oil imports to avoid new US tariffs risks pushing up fuel prices ahead of regional elections in India, or straining government finances.
"For some countries it is very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources," Rubio said.
Rubio's two-day visit to India will include a meeting with foreign minister S. Jaishankar on Tuesday to discuss bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade and investment, and defence.
A trade deal between India and the United States has been in the making for months but could not be finalised as talks stalled in part due to complications from the new tariff threat.
"The decision to pause on Russia sanctions could be the confidence-building measure that gives the two sides the negotiating space to get over the final hump," said Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council in Washington.
A trade deal has also been held back because Washington is yet to complete a Section 301 trade investigation into several nations, including India, over alleged excess manufacturing capacity. Section 301 is a US trade law that allows retaliation against unfair foreign trade practices.
Earlier this month, India joined a US-led initiative to act against structural overcapacity, along with a few other nations.
Trade officials in New Delhi last week said an agreement with the US was nearly done and expressed optimism over securing a tariff lower than those of competing countries — a longstanding Indian expectation from the deal.
"It (the waiver) provides an important opening and at a critical moment" after renewed tensions over the sanctions bill and new US visa policies had put the relationship "in danger of falling into even harder times," Kugelman said.

high_priority_articles.title: India-US trade deal influenced Trump to waive Russia oil sanctions, Rubio says - India Weekly
high_priority_articles.summary: India-US trade deal influenced Trump to waive Russia oil sanctions, Rubio says  India Weekly
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Highlights:
The United States considered its nearly finalized trade deal with India when deciding to waive sanctions targeting buyers of Russian oil, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday (19), signaling how energy security and bilateral economic ties are shaping Washington’s approach to New Delhi.
“We’re trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that. So that’s one of the things we’ve taken into consideration..” Rubio said during a press conference in Uzbekistan on Monday (19).
His remarks offer a significant indication that India-US trade negotiations were among the factors considered in Washington’s decision to pause provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The move has eased the immediate threat of steep US tariffs linked to purchases of Russian oil, a major point of contention between the two countries.
For India, the decision comes amid mounting pressure to secure affordable energy supplies while managing rising domestic inflation. It also offers a potential opening for New Delhi and Washington to resolve a key obstacle to their trade agreement.
Why India’s Russian oil purchases matter
India’s dependence on imported energy has made Russian crude a sensitive issue in its relationship with Washington. The United States has sought to pressure Moscow over its war against Ukraine, while India has maintained that its energy procurement decisions must account for domestic requirements, market conditions and the availability of alternative suppliers.
Rubio acknowledged that countries face different constraints when sourcing energy and said those realities must inform US foreign policy.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries. I know diesel prices are high in the United States, but they’re really, really high in a bunch of other countries around the world, and then we have to manage all of these things,” he said.
He added that replacing Russian energy supplies is not equally straightforward for every country.
“That’s not an excuse, but all that has to be balanced when you make foreign policy,” Rubio said.
His comments suggest that Washington’s approach is being shaped not only by its objective of pressuring Russia but also by the economic consequences of restricting energy supplies for countries that rely on them.
Trade negotiations and energy security intersect
The potential trade agreement has gained added importance as both governments work to narrow their differences over tariffs and market access. The threat of 100 per cent US tariffs linked to Russian oil purchases had emerged as a major sticking point in negotiations.
Rubio emphasized that Washington’s foreign policy calculations extend beyond the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
“The foreign policy of the United States, of course, takes into account what’s happening with the war between Russia and Ukraine, but it is not solely dominated by that. It hasn’t taken into account a variety of other factors, including our bilateral relationships with other countries, and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies. You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that’s the complex part of having to balance all this,” he said.
For New Delhi, the comments reinforce the importance of framing energy purchases as a matter of national economic stability rather than solely as a geopolitical choice.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs has said the government remains committed to ensuring energy security “through diversified sourcing and based on evolving market dynamics.” It has also said the implications of the proposed US legislation for bilateral relations and global energy markets were raised in discussions with American representatives.
Rising fuel prices add pressure
The sanctions decision comes as both countries face domestic concerns over energy costs and inflation. In the United States, diesel prices averaged $6.18 per gallon as of October 12, up from $3.48 at the beginning of the year, according to figures cited by the Council on Foreign Relations and the US Energy Information Administration.
India is also facing inflationary pressures. Retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September from 4.83 per cent in August, while food inflation increased to 7.74 per cent, according to the figures cited in the report.
Higher energy costs can place additional pressure on households, businesses and policymakers, making access to reliable supplies an important economic consideration for New Delhi.
Rubio is expected to visit Mumbai on October 20 for talks with India's external affairs minister S. Jaishankar. The discussions will take place as both countries seek to advance their trade negotiations and manage differences over India’s energy ties with Russia.
While Rubio’s remarks do not confirm that a trade agreement is imminent or that the sanctions waiver guarantees a final deal, they make clear that Washington has considered its relationship with India in weighing its Russia-related policy. For New Delhi, the immediate priority remains securing energy supplies while converting the diplomatic opening into progress on trade.

MADRID – Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.
Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.
Recommended Videos
Young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”
Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in NATO countries.
Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing on his Truth Social platform: “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” on Monday.
Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other elements including black-clad, masked agitators have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants.
Here's a look at what's driving the unrest:
Students say education resources are dwindling
In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they call understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.
The protests then broadened as France's CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.
Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.
In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.
Unaffordable housing stymies young people
In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.

Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea Backs Chip Suppliers with $1.5B Guarantee, Shared Production Lab - Tech Times
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea Backs Chip Suppliers with $1.5B Guarantee, Shared Production Lab  Tech Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea and SK Hynix signed a ₩2 trillion guarantee agreement (approximately $1.5 billion) for domestic semiconductor materials, components, and equipment suppliers on Monday, deploying a government credit-leverage mechanism that the companies feeding the world's AI memory supply chain have struggled to access from ordinary banks.
The signing of the Export Supply Chain Strengthening Guarantee took place at SK Hynix's Yongin Cluster exhibition center in Gyeonggi Province, with CEO Kwak Noh-jung, Trade, Industry and Energy Minister Kim Jeong-kwan, representatives from the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation (K-SURE) and the four largest commercial banks — KB Kookmin, Shinhan, Woori, and Hana — and a cohort of materials, components, and equipment (MCE) supplier companies in attendance. First guarantee certificates were presented to qualifying suppliers at the ceremony.
The Ministry of Industry called the agreement the largest trade-finance deal of its kind involving a single company, and Minister Kim stated there was a need to accelerate the expansion of the semiconductor industry's domestic production capacity while stressing that construction safety must remain a priority.
Why Korean Chip Suppliers Cannot Get Ordinary Bank Financing
The guarantee program exists because South Korea's chip supply ecosystem faces a problem that no amount of fab expansion by Samsung or SK Hynix automatically solves: the hundreds of small to mid-sized companies that supply specialty gases, photoresists, CMP polishing compounds, deposition equipment, and inspection tools operate on thin balance sheets and limited access to credit. When SK Hynix's own expansion schedule accelerates — as it has throughout 2025 and 2026 — those supplier order books can swell faster than their working capital. South Korea's broader policy response to this fragility has included a ₩5 trillion national semiconductor investment fund announced in August.
But the deeper problem is not credit risk — it is information. A small Korean materials company that develops a new photoresist formulation suited for SK Hynix's next-generation HBM production cannot simply bring it to a bank and ask for a development loan. The bank cannot evaluate whether the material will pass SK Hynix's internal qualification standards, because qualification requires time on an actual running production line, in an environment that mirrors mass-production conditions. Without that qualification data, no lender can accurately price the credit risk, so lenders over-discount it — or decline entirely. The company cannot commercialize the material, which means it cannot generate the revenue needed to attract financing, which means it never gets on the fab line to generate the qualification data. This chicken-and-egg bottleneck is the structural problem Monday's two-part program is designed to fix.
How the 20x Leverage Mechanism Works
The financial structure addresses the risk-pricing half of the problem through leverage, not subsidy. SK Hynix and the four commercial banks together contribute a combined ₩100 billion (approximately $67 million) in capital to the program. The Korea Trade Insurance Corporation — South Korea's export credit agency — amplifies that contribution at 20-to-1, providing guarantees covering up to ₩2 trillion in supplier loans. The resulting terms significantly improve on standard K-SURE program limits across every dimension.
Under the enhanced terms, qualifying MCE suppliers receive expanded loan limits (raised 50% above what other industries receive under standard K-SURE programs), a guarantee ratio raised from 90% to 100% of the loan amount, an extended term of three years rather than the standard one, and interest rate cuts of up to 2.5 percentage points. The guarantee fee — typically borne by the borrower — is reduced by 25 to 35 percent by K-SURE, with the participating banks covering the residual for the full three years.
The mechanism is a formal instance of what K-SURE calls its SMILE program — Supply-chain Miracle by Leverage. The same structure, at a smaller scale, backed ₩630 billion in guarantees for Hyundai Motor Group's automotive suppliers in August 2025 after US tariffs disrupted that supply chain; extending it to semiconductors, and nearly tripling the scale, signals that Seoul has elevated chip supply-chain fragility to a strategic priority equivalent to automotive disruption. The government has stated it plans to extend the program to defense, nuclear energy, and biotechnology sectors, targeting a combined ₩10 trillion in guarantees by year-end.
Trinity Fab: Solving the Lab Access Problem
The guarantee mechanism handles credit risk transfer. The information asymmetry problem — the missing fab-validation data — is addressed by a separate facility announced alongside the guarantee program.
The Trinity Fab is a process-demonstration facility of approximately 3,300 square meters (roughly 35,500 square feet) being built inside the Y1 fab building at the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster. Backed by a ₩870 billion (approximately $580 million) joint investment from the central government, Gyeonggi Province, and SK Hynix, Trinity Fab is designed to give MCE suppliers access to a real semiconductor manufacturing environment — with the same process conditions as a mass-production line — where newly developed materials and equipment can be characterized and qualified without consuming commercial fab capacity.
SK Hynix has framed the facility explicitly as infrastructure for technological independence. Ceremony participants on Monday toured both the Trinity Fab site and the adjacent construction of the Y1 fab itself, which is scheduled to begin initial cleanroom operations in February 2027 — pulled forward from an earlier May 2027 target — and is intended to produce sixth-generation 10-nanometer-class (1c) DRAM and support HBM4E, the company's next-generation high-bandwidth memory chip for AI accelerator customers.
Trinity Fab is targeted to open in 2027. When it does, a Korean specialty gas or photoresist maker will be able to characterize its new formulation under production conditions, generate the qualification data that SK Hynix's engineers need to approve it for use, and return to a lender with that data as evidence of commercial viability — closing the information loop that the guarantee program alone cannot close.
"To secure the global competitiveness of South Korea's semiconductor industry at the national level and further strengthen the status of K-semiconductors, building a solid materials, parts and equipment ecosystem is essential," CEO Kwak said at the signing. "Based on support from this export supply chain fund and the creation of a one-stop technology verification environment through the Trinity Fab, we will join forces with our partners to further solidify technology leadership in the global semiconductor market."
What It Takes to Build One HBM Stack
Understanding why the MCE supplier ecosystem matters requires understanding what goes into a High Bandwidth Memory chip — the product at the center of South Korea's AI hardware dominance.
HBM is a three-dimensional memory architecture in which multiple thin DRAM silicon dies are stacked vertically, connected through thousands of microscopic Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) that run through the stacked layers like vertical wire bundles. The resulting stack is then placed on a silicon interposer adjacent to the host processor — typically an Nvidia GPU or a hyperscaler's AI accelerator — enabling data bandwidth that conventional memory could never achieve through a flat 2D layout. HBM3E, the current production standard, delivers approximately 1,229 gigabytes per second of bandwidth per stack; an eight-stack configuration yields roughly 9.8 terabytes per second.
SK Hynix pioneered HBM alongside AMD and now holds an estimated 53 to 58 percent HBM share globally. That dominance is built on successive generations of process refinement — and each new generation requires a fresh cycle of materials and equipment qualification. The CMP polishing compounds used to flatten each layer must be re-validated. The etch gases used to drill the TSV holes must perform consistently at new geometries. The photoresists that define circuit patterns must meet tighter specifications. Every one of those cycles requires fab time that MCE suppliers cannot otherwise access.
SK Hynix holds approximately 70% of Nvidia's HBM4 supply allocation for the Vera Rubin platform in 2026, according to analyst estimates, and generated first-half 2026 revenue of approximately $86.6 billion. The MCE suppliers that the guarantee program is designed to protect are the upstream companies that make the materials enabling that scale.
Why This Problem Is Harder for Korea Than for China
The information asymmetry and financing gap that South Korea is addressing through market mechanisms — credit leverage, shared validation infrastructure — is a structural problem that China's semiconductor industry does not face in the same way. Chinese chipmakers such as YMTC and CXMT operate within a state-ownership system that allows them to mandate adoption of domestic materials and equipment, providing domestically developed products with access to production environments as a matter of policy rather than commercial negotiation. Chinese MCE developers do not need to generate qualification data to attract financing, because the state can direct adoption before qualification is complete.
South Korea cannot use administrative mandates. SK Hynix is a publicly listed company. Its procurement decisions are commercially driven and subject to the same competitive logic that makes Korean chips attractive to Nvidia: they have to be the best available at acceptable cost. high_priority_articles.full_text:
Supply Tightness Persists into Year-End
The global memory market remains undersupplied heading into the final quarter of 2026, a condition driven primarily by continued capital deployment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Data centre operators are absorbing high-bandwidth memory modules faster than manufacturers can scale output, creating pricing leverage for the two South Korean chip giants that dominate production.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together control more than 70 per cent of global DRAM capacity and roughly half of NAND Flash production. Both companies have reported that spot and contract negotiations for fourth-quarter deliveries reflect tightening availability, with lead times extending beyond historical norms. The undersupply environment marks a reversal from the inventory overhang that weighed on memory prices through much of 2024 and early 2025.
Industry data shows that contract prices for both DRAM and NAND Flash have climbed sequentially for three consecutive quarters. Samsung Electronics disclosed in its most recent earnings briefing that average selling prices for server DRAM rose by double-digit percentages quarter-on-quarter, while SK Hynix reported similar trajectories for its high-bandwidth memory products. The pricing momentum is expected to carry into the first half of 2027, barring a sharp pullback in data centre capital expenditure.
AI Infrastructure Drives Structural Shift
The memory shortage is not a cyclical blip but reflects structural changes in demand composition. Hyperscale cloud providers and enterprise AI labs are deploying large language models and machine learning workloads that require memory subsystems several times denser than traditional server configurations. High-bandwidth memory, particularly HBM3 and the forthcoming HBM3E variants, commands premium pricing and longer production cycles, leaving less capacity available for commodity DRAM.
SK Hynix has pivoted aggressively toward HBM, allocating more than half of its advanced fabrication capacity to these products. Samsung Electronics, while maintaining a broader portfolio, has similarly expanded HBM output and secured design wins with multiple hyperscale customers. Both companies are investing in new fabrication lines, but meaningful capacity additions are not expected until late 2027 or early 2028, prolonging the supply-demand imbalance.
NAND Flash is experiencing parallel dynamics. Data centre operators are upgrading storage arrays to support larger training datasets and inference workloads, driving demand for enterprise-grade SSDs. Consumer electronics, by contrast, remain sluggish; smartphone and PC shipments in Asia-Pacific markets have underperformed forecasts throughout 2026. The bifurcation means that memory manufacturers are prioritising higher-margin data centre products over consumer channels, further tightening availability in the former.
Price Ceiling from Long-Term Agreements
Despite favourable supply conditions, revenue upside for Samsung and SK Hynix faces constraints from contractual structures. A significant portion of memory sales to hyperscale customers is governed by long-term agreements that include price caps or formulaic escalation clauses. These contracts, typically spanning 12 to 24 months, were negotiated when memory prices were depressed and reflected customer efforts to lock in predictable costs.
As spot prices have risen above LTA ceilings, memory manufacturers have limited ability to capture full market pricing for contracted volumes. Samsung Electronics acknowledged in recent analyst calls that LTA provisions will dampen average selling price growth even as spot transactions command premiums. SK Hynix has indicated similar dynamics, noting that contract renewals scheduled for early 2027 will offer opportunities to reset pricing baselines, but current-year revenue will reflect older agreements.
The price cap mechanism also creates strategic tension. Hyperscale customers are hesitant to renegotiate terms mid-contract, fearing that concessions will erode their bargaining position in future cycles. Memory manufacturers, meanwhile, are reluctant to alienate key accounts by pushing too aggressively on price, given the concentrated nature of data centre demand. This standoff is likely to keep a lid on margin expansion in the near term, even as volume growth remains robust.
Regional Capacity and Geopolitical Considerations
South Korea's memory industry operates within a broader geopolitical context that influences investment decisions and supply chain configuration. Both Samsung and SK Hynix maintain the majority of their advanced fabrication capacity on the Korean peninsula, with some NAND production in China. Export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology transfer restrictions have complicated plans to expand Chinese operations, pushing new investment toward domestic sites or allied jurisdictions.
Japan and Taiwan have emerged as alternative locations for packaging and testing facilities, particularly for HBM products that require tight integration with logic dies. SK Hynix has established partnerships with TSMC for advanced packaging, while Samsung is expanding its own packaging capacity in South Korea. These moves reflect a strategic shift toward vertical integration and geographic diversification, reducing reliance on any single production node.
Southeast Asian markets, meanwhile, represent both a demand growth vector and a potential assembly hub. Singapore and Malaysia host significant data centre capacity, and memory manufacturers are exploring local partnerships to shorten logistics chains. However, advanced fabrication remains concentrated in Northeast Asia, and no immediate plans exist to transfer leading-edge DRAM or NAND production to the region.
Outlook and Market Positioning
Analyst consensus for 2027 points to high single-digit to low double-digit revenue growth for Samsung Electronics' semiconductor division and SK Hynix, driven primarily by memory products. Operating margin expansion is expected to be more modest, constrained by the factors outlined above. Both companies are also navigating the transition to next-generation process nodes, which entail higher capital intensity and longer ramp periods.
The consumer electronics recovery, if it materialises, could provide additional upside, but visibility remains limited. Smartphone demand in China has been weaker than anticipated, and PC refresh cycles tied to new operating system launches have not generated the expected memory content growth. For now, data centre infrastructure remains the dominant narrative, and memory manufacturers are aligning product roadmaps and capacity allocation accordingly.
Long-term, the memory market's centre of gravity is shifting toward AI and cloud infrastructure, a trend that favours suppliers with advanced technology portfolios and strong customer relationships. Samsung and SK Hynix are well positioned in this environment, but sustained leadership will require continued investment in R&D, process technology, and supply chain resilience. The next 18 months will test their ability to balance volume growth with pricing discipline in a market that rewards scale and technical differentiation in equal measure.

NSRC said on the 19th that it has won an order for lithography equipment to be installed at Company P's local production fab in Taiwan. Lithography equipment is core equipment in the semiconductor front-end process that uses light to etch fine circuit patterns onto wafers, and it determines a fab's yield and precision.
The customer, Company P, is a Taiwanese integrated device manufacturer (IDM) that produces MOSFETs, diodes, Schottky diodes, and insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs). The company's power semiconductors are supplied to large US AI data centers and used as core components in power conversion and distribution facilities, server cooling systems, and power supply units (PSUs). They are the foundational components that keep power supply, conversion, distribution, and cooling operating smoothly within data centers.
The contract is significant in that NSRC converted the technical expertise accumulated in South Korea's semiconductor equipment modification and refurbishment business, along with its network of overseas partners in the US, China, and Japan, into an actual overseas order. The company views its ability to handle the entire process — not just equipment procurement but also installation, verification, setup, and maintenance — as the competitive edge of its refurbishment business, and has recently hired a number of process and equipment engineers from major South Korean semiconductor companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
"With the spread of AI data centers, power supply and cooling efficiency have emerged as key challenges, and demand for power semiconductors and the equipment to produce them is rising rapidly," a company official said. "Through the lithography equipment order for Company P, we have entered the global AI data center value chain, and we expect orders for equipment related to AI data center power semiconductor manufacturing to expand in the second half of this year and into next year."
NSRC plans to use this order as a springboard to make a full-scale push into the power semiconductor equipment market. It expects that as AI data centers multiply, server power consumption will grow and power management will become more important, driving expanded production facility investment by power semiconductor makers. As power consumption and heat dissipation emerge as core challenges for AI infrastructure, new line expansions and process equipment orders from global power semiconductor companies are moving in tandem.

The recent weakness in chip stocks is attributed in part to questions over whether Big Tech's data center spending will translate into actual profits. Rising U.S. Treasury yields, currency volatility and inflation concerns have also weighed on risk appetite. In a report, Lee Soo-rim, an analyst at DS Investment & Securities, said "the recent market plunge centered on semiconductors reflects a combination of interest rates, inflation, exchange rates and concerns over slowing AI investment," adding that "physical semiconductor demand remains strong, but the market is applying a higher discount rate to the sustainability of that demand."
Concerns over the rise of China's largest DRAM maker, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), added to the losses. On Oct. 9, CXMT said it would launch a 4F² server DRAM within the year, cutting cell area by about 33% compared with the existing 6F² structure. Since Samsung Electronics aims to mass-produce 4F² DRAM on sub-10-nanometer nodes by 2028, fears spread that the Chinese company is narrowing the technology gap faster than expected. On Oct. 16, CXMT forecast third-quarter revenue of CNY 114.7 billion to CNY 119.7 billion (approximately $17.2 billion to approximately $17.9 billion), up 589-619% from a year earlier, and net profit of CNY 53.4 billion to CNY 54.9 billion (approximately $8.0 billion to approximately $8.2 billion), swinging to a profit.
Still, some on Wall Street argue the selloff was excessive. Kevin Cassidy, an analyst at Rosenblatt, raised the possibility that CXMT's 4F² cell is a "paper tiger," noting that given CXMT's process technology, the cell could be about 34% larger than rivals' existing 6F² products. Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho, also noted that CXMT has not disclosed full specifications or verified yields, making it difficult to directly compare its year-end product launch with Samsung Electronics' 2028 mass-production target.
Actual investment indicators, however, are improving. On Oct. 14, market research firm TrendForce raised its capex forecast for the world's nine largest cloud service providers (CSPs). Combined spending is expected to surge 106% year over year to $957 billion in 2026 and exceed $1.5 trillion in 2027. The 2027 growth forecast was raised to 60% from 50%. The revision reflects CSPs pulling forward spending due to higher server system prices, rising quotes amid component shortages, and prepayments demanded by some component suppliers. AI server shipment growth is also expected to accelerate to about 36% next year from 32.2% this year. AI server revenue is projected to grow more than 90% year over year to about $920 billion in 2027, accounting for 81% of the total server market.
Christophe Fouquet, chief executive of Dutch chip equipment maker ASML, said in the company's earnings release the same day that customers are showing interest in ordering equipment for supply in 2029-2030. He said supply plans for 2027-2028 alone would struggle to meet customer demand, and that ASML is considering expanding 2028 capacity beyond the previously flagged 30% increase. ASML's third-quarter revenue was €11.66 billion (approximately $13.1 billion) and net profit was €4.96 billion (approximately $5.6 billion), beating the market estimate of €4.1 billion (approximately $4.6 billion), while its full-year revenue forecast was raised to €44 billion-€45 billion (approximately $49.3 billion-$50.4 billion).
DS Investment & Securities believes concerns that the industry cycle could turn down after 2028 are excessively priced into current share prices. "Now is the time to use the market's excessive pessimism to increase exposure," Lee said. "It is excessive to price in fears of an earnings collapse like in the past." The view is that with earnings forecasts holding steady while valuations and supply-demand conditions have deteriorated simultaneously, the current situation could be a buying opportunity for medium-term investors.
Another supporting factor is that the earnings floor has risen compared with the past. As high-bandwidth memory (HBM) accounts for a larger share of revenue, companies can defend a certain level of profitability even in a downturn, the analysis says. Rising average selling prices for HBM4E, which is being adopted in Nvidia's custom next-generation products, is cited as a driver that will lift industry-wide profit in 2027. HBM is driven more by customer product roadmaps and contract terms than by short-term spot market supply and demand, meaning it faces less downward price pressure than commodity DRAM even in a downturn.
Nvidia's push to co-design the base die for its in-house HBM, NVHBM, with Samsung Electronics and TSMC also supports the durability of HBM demand. If the base die absorbs the memory controller previously housed in the GPU and cuts the physical-layer area by 60% versus standard HBM, bandwidth could widen by up to 30% and power consumption fall by 15%. Nvidia's choice of TSMC's 3-nanometer process comes down to density and yield. The industry sees TSMC's 3nm yield at above 90% and Samsung Foundry's 2nm (SF2) yield at around 60%. TSMC plans to add two 3nm lines at Fab 18 in Tainan, Taiwan, targeting mass production in the first half of 2027 and the first half of 2028, while its second Arizona fab targets the third quarter of 2027 and its second Kumamoto, Japan, fab targets 2028. UBS estimates HBM demand next year at about 61.5 billion gigabits, up 91% from this year, while new supply will reach only 54.6 billion gigabits, leaving a shortfall of about 10%.
As its base case, DS Investment & Securities assumes DRAM ASPs fall 20% in 2028, 10% in 2029 and 5% in 2030. Even in that scenario, operating profit at Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix would decline only 7-12% and 12-18%, respectively, from 2027 levels, according to the estimates. A separate price-sensitivity analysis found that if the cumulative three-year decline in DRAM ASPs stays at 32% and NAND at 39%, the companies could retain 80-90% of their 2027 profit.

high_priority_articles.summary: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited  The GuardianHouthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say  BBCIran war updates: 58 recruits killed, 200 hurt in Houthi attacks in Yemen  Al JazeeraHouthi rebels strike Yemen’s government forces, killing at least 53  AP NewsHouthi attack kills 58 at Yemen government training camp, governor says  Reuters
high_priority_articles.full_text:
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.
